chunks.title: Accessibility conformance report (draft)
chunks.heading: Accessibility conformance report (draft)
chunks.text: See how ravonics.com conforms to WCAG 2.1 AA and Section 508, and on what evidence. Accessibility conformance report (draft) Draft Section 508 / WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility conformance report (VPAT 2.x format) for the ravonics.com public website. Read related work Engage with team VPAT 2.x · WCAG 2.1 edition · Draft Report scope Product: the ravonics.com public website (all published routes). Standards: WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA, which Section 508 (36 CFR 1194) incorporates for web content. Evaluated: 2026-11-22. Contact: contact@ravonics.com . Evaluation methods Every change to the site runs a route contract in continuous integration: each published route is loaded in Chromium and checked with axe-core for WCAG A and AA rules, a single main landmark and h1, a page title, broken images, horizontal overflow and reflow at 320 pixels wide. On the main contact routes a keyboard walk checks that the Tab key reaches every control, leaves the page after the last one and shows where focus is. Criteria marked Not Evaluated still need a manual review with keyboard and screen-reader testing. This report is a draft until that review is complete; it will not claim more than the evidence shows. Summary: 14 Supports · 29 Not Evaluated · 4 Not Applicable · 3 Partially Supports across 50 Level A and AA success criteria.

chunks.title: Quantum Technologies - QKD, Quantum Computing, Quantum Sensing | DoW Quantum Contractor
chunks.heading: Quantum Technologies
chunks.text: Quantum Technologies Capabilities Quantum Technologies Advanced AI Autonomous Systems Autonomy Software Computer Vision Intelligence & Decision Tactical Communications Quantum Technologies Cryptography & Blockchain High-Performance Computing Systems Engineering Quantum Computing & Communications for Next-Generation Defense Quantum technologies unlock computational and communications capabilities beyond what classical systems can provide. We apply quantum algorithms to optimization and cryptographic analysis, and build toward quantum key distribution architectures designed to stay ahead of emerging quantum threats. Our partner INSTAR Lab's physics bench, led by researchers in condensed-matter and materials science, supports applied quantum research in post-quantum cryptography aligned to NIST FIPS 203, 204, and 205. Leveraging quantum mechanics to deliver computational and communications superiority. Key Capabilities Quantum Computing & Programming Quantum algorithm development for optimization, simulation, and cryptanalysis using gate-based systems and quantum annealing platforms with exponential speedups over classical computing. Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) Quantum key distribution architectures engineered to protect communications against interception, leveraging photon-based key exchange designed so any eavesdropping attempt is detectable in principle. Quantum Communications Networks Quantum repeaters and satellite-based QKD networks enabling ultra-secure tactical and strategic communications across global distances with quantum entanglement. Quantum Sensing & Metrology Atomic clocks and quantum sensors delivering unprecedented precision for navigation, timing, and detection, critical for GPS-denied operations and submarine detection. Quantum Algorithm Development Custom quantum circuits and variational algorithms for logistics optimization, molecular simulation, and machine learning acceleration with quantum advantage. Hybrid Quantum-Classical Systems Integrated platforms combining quantum processors with classical HPC for near-term quantum advantage in defense applications without requiring fault-tolerant quantum computing.

chunks.text: Autonomy Software Capabilities Autonomy Software Advanced AI Autonomous Systems Autonomy Software Computer Vision Intelligence & Decision Tactical Communications Quantum Technologies Cryptography & Blockchain High-Performance Computing Systems Engineering Autonomy Software for Robotic Platforms in Extreme Operating Environments Robotic platforms extend operational reach into environments that are too hazardous or inaccessible for direct human presence. From unmanned aerial vehicles conducting ISR missions to ground robots supporting explosive ordnance disposal, we build the autonomy software and integration that enables these systems to perform in demanding conditions. Our software stack pairs learned manipulation and mobility policies with assurance tooling and human-robot teaming frameworks designed to keep operators in control. Assured autonomy software for robotic platforms and swarms operating across multi-domain, contested battlespaces. Key Capabilities Multi-Domain Unmanned Platforms From aerial ISR drones to ground reconnaissance robots and underwater autonomous vehicles. Our software powers unmanned systems across every operational domain, hardened for contested conditions. Robot Foundation Model Stack We adapt vision-language-action models so one learned policy can drive arms and end-effectors across many tasks, from EOD operations to precision assembly, with force feedback. Human-Robot Teaming Our frameworks let one operator direct many machines under structured human oversight, with readable autonomy that shows why a robot acted, so crews keep tactical control of robotic reach.

chunks.title: Tactical Communications - Anti-Jam SDR, Resilient MANET, LPI Waveforms | DoW Networks
chunks.heading: Tactical Communications Systems
chunks.text: Tactical Communications Systems Capabilities Tactical Communications Systems Advanced AI Autonomous Systems Autonomy Software Computer Vision Intelligence & Decision Tactical Communications Quantum Technologies Cryptography & Blockchain High-Performance Computing Systems Engineering Resilient Tactical Networks for Contested Battlespaces Tactical communications infrastructure forms the connectivity backbone for multi-domain operations, supporting command and control in GPS-denied and electronically contested environments. From resilient mesh networks to anti-jamming waveforms, we engineer communications systems designed to operate when adversaries attempt disruption or interception. Our designs integrate with existing defense networks and are built toward JADC2-compatible architectures, leveraging zero-trust networking aligned to NIST 800-207. Resilient communications architectures engineered to maintain connectivity when adversaries attempt disruption. Key Capabilities Resilient Tactical Mesh Networks Self-healing mobile ad-hoc networks with adaptive routing maintain secure communications in GPS-denied, jammed, or disconnected battlespace environments with automatic path reconfiguration. Anti-Jamming Waveforms Frequency-hopping spread spectrum and directional antennas defeat hostile electronic warfare, maintaining reliable communications despite sophisticated jamming attempts across contested spectrum. Software-Defined Radios (SDR) Reconfigurable waveforms and adaptive modulation schemes enable rapid response to changing operational requirements and electromagnetic environments without hardware replacement. Satellite Communications (SATCOM) Resilient beyond-line-of-sight connectivity through military SATCOM terminals with anti-jam capabilities, ensuring global reach for expeditionary operations and strategic command. Low Probability of Intercept (LPI) Covert communications using ultra-wideband and adaptive power control prevent adversary detection and direction-finding, critical for special operations and intelligence collection. Cross-Domain Gateway Integration Secure information exchange between tactical edge and strategic networks across multiple classification levels with automated data sanitization and access control.

chunks.title: AI Ethics in Defense: Autonomy, Accountability, and the Human-on-the-Loop Principle | Ravonics
chunks.heading: AI Ethics in Defense: Autonomy, Accountability, and the Human-on-the-Loop Principle
chunks.text: AI Ethics in Defense: Autonomy, Accountability, and the Human-on-the-Loop Principle Insights Industry Perspectives AI Ethics in Defense A Ravonics defense AI policy perspective on how DoW's ethical AI framework and the human-on-the-loop principle are reshaping what responsible AI procurement actually requires Defense AI is moving from research laboratory to acquisition program at a pace that has outrun the policy infrastructure designed to govern it. DoW's five ethical AI principles (responsible, equitable, traceable, reliable, and governable) were articulated in 2020 and affirmed through the Responsible AI Strategy and Implementation Pathway. DoW Directive 3000.09, updated in 2023, sets the policy framework for autonomous weapon systems and the human judgment requirements that must accompany them. Yet the gap between policy language and program-level implementation remains wide, and acquisition programs that do not engage with that gap early are increasingly encountering friction at test and evaluation, milestone reviews, and Congressional oversight. The ethical AI conversation in defense is not primarily a philosophical one; it is an acquisition policy conversation. The questions that matter at program level are concrete: What level of human control is required for this system's intended use? What does the program office need to demonstrate to satisfy DoW Directive 3000.09 review requirements? How is accountability assigned when an AI-enabled decision leads to an unintended outcome? What does "traceable" mean in practice for a machine learning model that produces recommendations under time pressure? The following six dimensions frame the policy landscape that defense AI programs must navigate in 2026 and beyond.

chunks.title: AI Ethics in Defense: Autonomy, Accountability, and the Human-on-the-Loop Principle | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Human-on-the-Loop vs. Human-in-the-Loop: The Distinction That Matters
chunks.text: Human-on-the-Loop vs. Human-in-the-Loop: The Distinction That Matters The distinction between human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop control is not semantic; it is the organizing axis of DoW's autonomy policy. Human-in-the-loop means a human must affirmatively authorize each consequential action; the system cannot act without that authorization in the decision cycle. Human-on-the-loop means the system can act autonomously within defined parameters, but a human retains the ability to monitor, intervene, and override. DoW Directive 3000.09 governs which category applies to which class of autonomous and semi-autonomous weapon systems, and the classification has direct implications for what legal review, operational concept approval, and commander accountability a program requires. Blurring this distinction in program documentation (describing a human-on-the-loop system as having "human oversight" without specifying the actual control architecture) is the single most common source of friction at 3000.09 legal and policy reviews. DoW's Five Ethical AI Principles as Acquisition Requirements DoW's ethical AI principles are not aspirational statements; they translate into testable acquisition requirements when a program team is serious about them. "Responsible" requires that a designated human be accountable for AI development and employment decisions. "Equitable" requires testing for bias across the populations and operating conditions the system will encounter. "Traceable" requires that the system's methodology be auditable and its outputs explicable to the humans relying on them. "Reliable" requires that the system perform within defined boundaries under expected and unexpected conditions. "Governable" requires that the system can be deactivated, adjusted, or overridden. Each of these generates specific test and evaluation requirements that must be scoped into a program's T&E strategy well before milestone B if they are not to become schedule-breaking late discoveries.

chunks.title: AI Ethics in Defense: Autonomy, Accountability, and the Human-on-the-Loop Principle | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Accountability Chains Cannot Be Diffused by Algorithmic Complexity
chunks.text: Accountability Chains Cannot Be Diffused by Algorithmic Complexity A persistent challenge in defense AI acquisition is the tendency for accountability to become diffuse when a machine learning model sits between a human decision-maker and an outcome. Vendors sometimes implicitly rely on algorithmic opacity to limit their liability exposure. Program offices sometimes accept this opacity because it makes oversight easier to defer. Neither posture is legally or operationally sustainable. The law of armed conflict imposes accountability on commanders for actions taken by systems under their control. That accountability cannot be delegated to an algorithm. Programs that design accountability chains from the outset (who is responsible for training data quality, who approves the operational parameters, who has authority to suspend the system) are better positioned at legal reviews and better equipped to investigate and learn from incidents in the field. Test and Evaluation Must Include Adversarial and Out-of-Distribution Conditions Machine learning systems can perform with high measured accuracy on evaluation datasets while failing in ways that are unexpected and potentially consequential when they encounter inputs outside their training distribution. Defense operating environments are specifically designed by adversaries to create out-of-distribution conditions: sensor spoofing, environmental camouflage, electronic warfare, novel platform signatures. A T&E strategy for a defense AI system that evaluates only nominal performance against representative datasets is providing false confidence. The Responsible AI (RAI) guidelines from CDAO and the operational test and evaluation community increasingly expect programs to demonstrate adversarial robustness, failure mode characterization, and performance bounds across the full operational envelope, not just the favorable test conditions that maximize reported accuracy.

chunks.title: AI Ethics in Defense: Autonomy, Accountability, and the Human-on-the-Loop Principle | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Traceability and Explainability Are Not the Same Requirement
chunks.text: Traceability and Explainability Are Not the Same Requirement DoW's principle of traceability addresses two related but distinct needs that programs often conflate. Audit traceability means being able to reconstruct what data the model was trained on, what parameters were set, what version was deployed, and what inputs produced a specific output: the forensic record needed to investigate a decision after the fact. Explainability addresses the real-time need: can a human decision-maker understand why the system produced a recommendation well enough to exercise informed judgment about whether to act on it? These requirements differ in who needs them (auditors versus operators), when they are needed (post-hoc versus real-time), and what technical investment they require. Programs that design only for audit traceability while leaving operators without actionable explanations of system outputs are not meeting the intent of the principle. Responsible AI Is Becoming a Competitive Differentiator in Defense Procurement Congressional attention to autonomous systems, CDAO's expanding role in AI governance, and the growing sophistication of program executive offices in evaluating AI vendor claims are collectively raising the bar for what responsible AI means in a defense procurement context. Vendors who can demonstrate mature responsible AI practices (documented accountability chains, adversarial T&E results, explainability tooling appropriate to operator cognitive loads, and credible human control architectures) are increasingly distinguishable from those offering capable models without governance substance. For a new small business like Ravonics, positioning on responsible AI practice is not a hedge against capability claims; it is an honest reflection of the architectural discipline that federal AI programs actually require from solution providers.

chunks.title: Autonomous Platform Coordination: Swarm Intelligence Concepts | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Autonomous Platform Coordination: Swarm Intelligence Concepts
chunks.text: Autonomous Platform Coordination: Swarm Intelligence Concepts Insights Technical Publications Autonomous Platform Coordination A Ravonics and INSTAR Lab perspective on coordination that emerges from simple local rules, not central command Watch a murmuration of starlings at dusk and you witness thousands of birds producing one coherent, fluid shape, turning, folding, and reforming without a leader, a controller, or a master plan. Each bird follows only a few simple rules about its nearest neighbors: stay close, match heading, avoid collision. Coherent global behavior emerges from purely local interaction. Nature solved decentralized coordination long before we tried to engineer it. That observation reframes how we think about coordinating unmanned platforms. A centralized controller is elegant on a whiteboard and brittle in the field: jam the link, knock out the node, and the whole formation degrades. Swarm-inspired design instead distributes intelligence across many attritable platforms, each acting on local information. The result is autonomy that bends rather than breaks, keeping a human firmly in command of intent. The pillars below outline how we approach that design space. Emergent Behavior from Local Rules Sophisticated group behavior need not be centrally programmed. A small set of local rules (separation, alignment, cohesion) can produce search, screening, and coverage patterns at the formation level. We treat these rules as a design vocabulary: tune the simple interactions, and the useful global behavior follows, without a single platform ever needing the full picture.

chunks.title: Autonomous Platform Coordination: Swarm Intelligence Concepts | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Decentralized Control & No Single Point of Failure
chunks.text: Decentralized Control & No Single Point of Failure When no node is in charge, no node is indispensable. Authority and computation are spread across the formation so that losing platforms degrades capability gracefully rather than collapsing it. Attrition becomes a tolerable cost rather than a catastrophic one: a property that matters profoundly in contested environments where individual platforms are expected to be lost. Resilient Mesh Communication Coordination depends on platforms exchanging just enough state to stay coherent. A self-healing mesh, where each node relays for its neighbors, removes the central radio as a target and reroutes around jamming or loss. We favor terse, frequent local updates over heavy centralized telemetry, so the network stays useful even when bandwidth is scarce and links are intermittent. GPS-Denied / Contested-Environment Navigation Coordination cannot assume a satellite fix. Platforms must hold formation using relative positioning, inertial sensing, visual and terrain cues, and peer-to-peer ranging. By navigating relative to one another rather than to an external grid, a formation can remain coherent and purposeful through spoofing and denial of the signals adversaries most expect us to rely on. Distributed Sensing & Consensus Many modest sensors, fused across a formation, can outperform one exquisite platform. The architectural challenge is consensus: reconciling partial, noisy, sometimes conflicting observations into a shared picture without a central arbiter. Lightweight agreement protocols let the group converge on what it collectively believes while tolerating dropouts, disagreement, and degraded individual sensors.

chunks.title: Autonomous Platform Coordination: Swarm Intelligence Concepts | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Human-on-the-Loop Control & Accountability
chunks.text: Human-on-the-Loop Control & Accountability Decentralization governs how platforms coordinate, never whether a human remains accountable. The operator sets intent, constraints, and rules of engagement, monitors the formation, and retains authority to redirect or recall it through explicit handoff protocols. We design for meaningful human judgment over consequential actions, with ethical and legal constraints encoded as boundaries the system cannot cross on its own. chunks.title: Real-Time AI Decision Systems for Federal Missions | White Paper Abstract | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Real-Time AI Decision Systems for Federal Missions | White Paper Abstract
chunks.text: Real-Time AI Decision Systems for Federal Missions | White Paper Abstract Insights Technical Publications Real-Time AI Decision Systems A Ravonics architectural perspective on real-time AI design for federal missions Modern federal operations increasingly require AI-assisted decision-making at near-machine speed across interconnected domains. Designing systems that can process multi-source data, surface patterns, and support operator decisions in real-time is among the most demanding technical problems facing new entrants to the defense technology market. This forthcoming white paper draws on our leadership team's combined decades in computer science and AI/ML to outline the architectural considerations Ravonics brings to federal engagements. The following sections preview the key design pillars covered in the full paper: Latency-Optimized Architecture Design Federal mission systems demand sub-second inference times. The paper examines model quantization, pruning, and knowledge distillation as approaches to reduce neural network size without sacrificing accuracy, enabling capable AI on constrained tactical edge hardware. Resilient Data Pipeline Engineering Design must account for denied, degraded, intermittent, and limited (DDIL) environments. The paper covers local caching strategies, predictive pre-fetching, and graceful degradation patterns, ensuring no critical data is lost during network disruptions. Explainable AI for Operator Trust Federal operators need to understand why an AI recommends specific actions. The paper addresses attention visualization, SHAP values, and counterfactual explanations as UI-level mechanisms, including confidence scores and source attribution.

chunks.title: Real-Time AI Decision Systems for Federal Missions | White Paper Abstract | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Continuous Model Monitoring and Drift Detection
chunks.text: Continuous Model Monitoring and Drift Detection Input distributions shift over time as conditions change. The paper covers statistical process control approaches for detecting data drift and model degradation, with human-in-the-loop approval gates before any retraining is deployed. Security-First ML Pipeline Federal ML pipelines must guard against adversarial inputs and data poisoning. The paper addresses input validation, adversarial robustness, training data provenance tracking, and cryptographic signing of model artifacts: all prerequisites for operating within accredited security boundaries. Multi-Level Data Fusion Fusing data across sensitivity levels requires deliberate architectural separation. The paper examines one-way data guard patterns and cross-domain solution design to support inference workflows that span multiple sensitivity tiers without cross-contamination. Human-Machine Teaming Interfaces The paper's design philosophy is augmentation, not replacement. Interface patterns covered include adjustable automation levels, manual override capabilities, and explicit handoff protocols that preserve operator authority and accountability throughout the decision loop. chunks.title: CMMC 2.0: What Defense Contractors Must Understand Before First Award | Ravonics
chunks.heading: CMMC 2.0: What Defense Contractors Must Understand Before First Award
chunks.text: CMMC 2.0: What Defense Contractors Must Understand Before First Award Insights Industry Perspectives CMMC 2.0 & First Award A Ravonics perspective on what the CMMC 2.0 framework actually requires, written from the same vantage point as every new defense contractor pursuing the pathway for the first time The Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) 2.0 program became a contractual reality with the publication of the 48 CFR rule in late 2024. For defense contractors handling Federal Contract Information (FCI) or Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI), the pathway to award on DoW contracts increasingly runs through a demonstrated, documented, and in many cases independently assessed cybersecurity posture. The program is not new in intent (DFARS 252.204-7012 has required NIST SP 800-171 compliance since 2017), but CMMC 2.0 introduces formal verification requirements that self-attestation alone can no longer satisfy for higher-level contracts. Ravonics is itself pursuing this pathway as a new small business. Our NIST 800-171 alignment is underway and our CMMC assessment is planned. We hold no CMMC certification today. What we can offer is a clear-eyed account of what the framework actually requires, drawn from firsthand engagement with the assessment preparation process and the technical demands of NIST SP 800-171 implementation. Understanding the Three Levels and Which Applies to You CMMC 2.0 collapsed the original five-level model into three. Level 1 covers 17 basic safeguarding practices from FAR 52.204-21 and applies to contractors handling only FCI (not CUI). Level 2 aligns exactly to the 110 practices in NIST SP 800-171 and applies to contractors handling CUI; most DoW contracts with CUI flow-down will require Level 2. Level 3 adds 24 practices drawn from NIST SP 800-172 for contractors on the highest-priority programs. Determining which level applies starts with whether your work involves CUI and whether any solicitation clause (notably DFARS 252.204-7021) specifies a required level. Assuming Level 1 applies to any program touching DoW data is a risk posture that warrants reassessment.

chunks.title: CMMC 2.0: What Defense Contractors Must Understand Before First Award | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Self-Assessment vs. C3PAO: Who Assesses You
chunks.text: Self-Assessment vs. C3PAO: Who Assesses You Level 1 and some Level 2 contracts allow annual self-assessment, where a senior company official affirms compliance in the Supplier Performance Risk System (SPRS). Level 2 contracts designated as "critical" by the program office require a triennial third-party assessment by a CMMC Third Party Assessment Organization (C3PAO) certified by the CMMC Accreditation Body (Cyber AB). Level 3 requires a government-led assessment by DCSA. Contractors should identify early whether their target contract vehicle will require a C3PAO assessment, because the scheduling backlog and cost of a third-party assessment are material planning inputs, not last-minute concerns. NIST SP 800-171: The 110 Controls Beneath Level 2 NIST SP 800-171 Revision 2 defines 110 security requirements across 14 domains: access control, awareness and training, audit and accountability, configuration management, identification and authentication, incident response, maintenance, media protection, personnel security, physical protection, risk assessment, security assessment, system and communications protection, and system and information integrity. Revision 3 (published 2024) reorganizes and adds requirements; contractors should monitor which revision their assessment will reference. Each requirement must be implemented, documented, and demonstrable; "we plan to implement" is not compliant unless accompanied by a properly scoped Plan of Action and Milestones. SPRS Score, POA&M, and the 110-Point System SPRS (Supplier Performance Risk System) hosts a contractor's self-assessed score against the NIST SP 800-171 DoW Assessment Methodology. A perfect score is 110; each unimplemented practice carries a weighted deduction, with the most critical controls reducing the score the most steeply. A score below 110 must be accompanied by a Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) documenting the gap, the remediation approach, and the expected completion date. The SPRS score is visible to contracting officers and is a factor in contract award decisions. Contractors who submit a score without a credible, time-bounded POA&M for each gap are exposed to False Claims Act risk if the score is later found to have been submitted without a good-faith basis.

chunks.title: CMMC 2.0: What Defense Contractors Must Understand Before First Award | Ravonics
chunks.heading: CUI Scoping and Enclave Architecture
chunks.text: CUI Scoping and Enclave Architecture One of the most consequential decisions in CMMC preparation is defining the CUI boundary: the scope of systems, people, and processes that touch Controlled Unclassified Information. A broader CUI boundary means more systems in scope for the 110 controls, more devices to harden, more endpoints to monitor, and higher assessment cost. Many contractors reduce this burden through CUI enclave architecture: isolating CUI handling to a defined, hardened environment (dedicated endpoints, segmented network, strict access control) while keeping the broader business environment out of scope. The enclave must be technically enforced and consistently maintained; inspectors assess the actual environment, not the diagram. Flow-Down, Subcontractors, and Supply Chain Responsibility CMMC requirements flow down to subcontractors who handle CUI or FCI on the same program. A prime contractor who achieves Level 2 certification cannot satisfy program requirements if a subcontractor handling CUI operates without equivalent controls. The prime is responsible for including DFARS 252.204-7021 in subcontracts and for verifying that subcontractors have the required certification prior to award. Small businesses entering the defense supply chain as subcontractors should not assume CMMC is only the prime's problem; flow-down clauses make it everyone's obligation. Building the assessment and certification timeline into subcontract negotiations, rather than after task order award, avoids the most common schedule surprise.

chunks.title: Digital Twin Modeling for Multi-Domain Operations | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Digital Twin Modeling for Multi-Domain Operations
chunks.text: Digital Twin Modeling for Multi-Domain Operations Insights Research Directions Digital Twin Multi-Domain A Ravonics architectural perspective on digital twin patterns for multi-domain operational simulation: model synchronization, fidelity management, and verification approaches for federal programs The term "digital twin" has accumulated significant marketing weight across industries, but for defense and federal programs its technical meaning is precise: a continuously synchronized virtual representation of a physical system, environment, or operational construct, updated from live telemetry and capable of supporting simulation, analysis, prediction, and decision support. In multi-domain operations, where land, sea, air, space, and cyber activities must be coordinated as an integrated whole, the need for authoritative, synchronized virtual representations of force disposition, system state, and environmental conditions is acute. The alternative is fragmented situational awareness spread across domain-specific tools with incompatible data models. Building digital twins for multi-domain operational contexts is architecturally distinct from industrial IoT applications. The heterogeneity is extreme: platforms span ship combat systems, airborne sensors, ground vehicles, space assets, and cyber terrain. Update rates vary from milliseconds (fire control) to hours (logistics and sustainment status). Classification levels and network separation add additional complexity to data movement. And unlike a manufacturing floor where the physical system is fully owned and instrumented, military platforms are fielded independently by service programs with their own data models and interface standards. The sections below outline the architecture pillars that shape a credible approach.

chunks.title: Digital Twin Modeling for Multi-Domain Operations | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Model Architecture and Domain Scope
chunks.text: Model Architecture and Domain Scope A multi-domain digital twin is not a single monolithic model; it is a federation of domain-specific models (land force disposition, maritime picture, air tracks, space situational awareness, cyber terrain) composed through a shared data fabric and a common operational picture layer. Each domain model owns the authoritative representation of its assets, publishing state updates through well-defined interfaces. The federation layer resolves cross-domain dependencies: a strike package model must reference air, space (for GPS and ISR), and cyber (for network-enabled weapons) simultaneously. Defining the decomposition boundaries (which information lives in which domain model) is an architecture decision that shapes maintainability for the life of the program. Model-Telemetry Synchronization The defining property of a digital twin is synchronization with its physical counterpart. In multi-domain operations, telemetry arrives from heterogeneous sources: tactical data links (Link 16, VMF, JREAP), space tracking networks, cyber sensor feeds, and logistics systems. Synchronization architecture must handle variable latency, message loss, and conflicting reports of the same entity from different sources. A track management layer (analogous to the common operational picture fusion engines used in C2 systems) maintains entity state by reconciling multiple inbound updates using confidence weights, recency, and source authority rules. Divergence between the virtual model and the physical state must be detectable and flagged, not silently tolerated.

chunks.title: Digital Twin Modeling for Multi-Domain Operations | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Fidelity Levels and Computational Scaling
chunks.text: Fidelity Levels and Computational Scaling Not every component of an operational digital twin requires the same level of physical fidelity. High-fidelity simulation of individual platform subsystems (propulsion, sensors, weapons employment) is computationally expensive and appropriate for engineering analysis or specific engagement modeling. Operational-level twins that support course-of-action analysis and logistics planning operate at a higher level of abstraction: entities, capabilities, and constraint envelopes rather than physics-based subsystem simulation. Architecturally, fidelity levels should be selectable at runtime, allowing the same twin to serve both detailed engineering queries and rapid operational planning without maintaining two separate systems. Adaptive resolution (increasing fidelity in a geographic or functional area of interest while holding the surrounding context at low fidelity) is a key capability for computational tractability. Verification and Validation A digital twin whose outputs are not validated against real-world behavior is a simulation, not a twin. Verification establishes that the model correctly implements its specification; validation establishes that the model's outputs match observed physical reality within acceptable bounds. For multi-domain operational twins, validation is challenging because the physical system (a military operation) cannot be exhaustively exercised under controlled conditions. Approaches include back-testing against historical exercise telemetry, comparison against independent simulation tools, unit testing of domain model components against known analytical solutions, and red-team challenges that attempt to surface failure modes. Continuous validation (comparing twin predictions against observed outcomes as operations proceed) is the gold standard and requires an instrumentation and feedback loop that must be designed in from the start.

chunks.title: Digital Twin Modeling for Multi-Domain Operations | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Cross-Domain Data Movement and Security Architecture
chunks.text: Cross-Domain Data Movement and Security Architecture Multi-domain operational data spans multiple classification levels and network enclaves. A digital twin federation that aggregates space, cyber, and conventional force data must navigate data transfer authorities, cross-domain solutions, and need-to-know boundaries. Architecturally, this argues for domain models that are enclave-resident and publish only the authorized subset of their state to the federation layer: a push model with explicit release decisions, not a pull model where the federation queries any field it wants. Zero Trust principles (continuous verification of requestor identity and entitlement before each data access) are appropriate for the federation's API layer, consistent with the broader federal mandate for ZT adoption. Course-of-Action Analysis and Decision Support The decision-support value of a digital twin emerges when it can run ahead of real time: projecting force states under alternative courses of action, identifying logistics shortfalls before they become operational constraints, and evaluating how adversary actions in one domain propagate to others. This requires a simulation execution layer that can branch from the current synchronized state, run multiple COA variants concurrently, and return ranked outcomes within a planning timescale. The synchronization discipline established in normal operations is what makes COA branching credible; a twin that has drifted from physical reality produces misleading projections. Maintaining synchronization fidelity is therefore not just an operational requirement; it is a prerequisite for the analytic value the twin is meant to deliver.

chunks.title: Tactical Edge AI Hardware Evaluation | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Tactical Edge AI Hardware Evaluation
chunks.text: Tactical Edge AI Hardware Evaluation Insights Research Directions Edge AI Hardware Evaluation A Ravonics hardware perspective on evaluating COTS AI accelerator silicon (GPU, NPU, FPGA, DSP, and ASIC) against the SWaP, thermal, ruggedization, and supply-chain constraints that govern tactical edge deployment The tactical edge AI problem has two distinct layers. One layer is software: how to compress, optimize, and govern models so they run accurately within constrained compute budgets. The other layer (often underweighted in early program planning) is silicon: which physical accelerator hardware actually provides the throughput needed, within the power envelope available, surviving the temperatures and vibration profiles the mission environment demands, and available through supply chains that survive adversarial pressure on the semiconductor ecosystem. Choosing the wrong silicon early locks in SWaP penalties, thermal management costs, and software porting debt that persist for the life of the platform. This article focuses on the hardware evaluation layer. It is complementary to Ravonics' coverage of model optimization techniques; that discussion addresses how models are shaped to fit the hardware; this one addresses how hardware is selected, characterized, and validated for the mission. The dimensions below form the evaluation framework Ravonics applies when advising on edge AI hardware selection for federal programs.

chunks.title: Tactical Edge AI Hardware Evaluation | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Accelerator Taxonomy: GPU, NPU, FPGA, DSP, and ASIC
chunks.text: Accelerator Taxonomy: GPU, NPU, FPGA, DSP, and ASIC Each accelerator class represents a different point in the programmability-versus-efficiency trade-off space. Embedded GPUs (NVIDIA Jetson family, AMD Versal AI Edge) offer broad software ecosystem support and flexibility for general-purpose parallel workloads, at moderate power draw. Neural processing units (NPUs) are purpose-built for tensor operations, yielding superior efficiency on supported operator sets but narrower programmability. FPGAs enable custom datapath design and deterministic timing, valuable when the inference pipeline has unusual operator mixes or strict latency guarantees. DSPs serve signal-processing-heavy pipelines well. Custom ASICs achieve the highest efficiency but require volume commitments and multi-year development cycles incompatible with the pace of most defense programs. No single class wins; evaluation starts by matching the workload's operator profile to the silicon's native instruction set. Performance-per-Watt Benchmarking Methodology Aggregate throughput numbers (TOPS, TFLOPS) published by vendors measure peak theoretical performance on idealized workloads. Evaluation must use mission-representative benchmarks: the actual model architecture, precision levels, batch size, and input resolution the program will deploy. Sustained throughput under realistic duty cycles matters more than burst peak. Power measurement must capture the full platform draw (accelerator, host CPU, memory, and interconnect), not just the accelerator TDP. Thermal steady-state is equally important: a device that sustains 25 TOPS at 10W under bench conditions may throttle to 12 TOPS at 15W when the ambient temperature reflects a vehicle engine compartment in summer. Benchmark instrumentation must replicate the thermal environment, not just the compute workload.

chunks.title: Tactical Edge AI Hardware Evaluation | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Thermal Management and Environmental Hardening
chunks.text: Thermal Management and Environmental Hardening Commercial edge AI modules are often qualified to industrial temperature ranges (-40°C to 85°C junction), but tactical platforms may exceed these bounds during extended operations in desert environments, or impose convection constraints that prevent fan-based cooling entirely. Evaluating thermal dissipation paths (conduction through chassis walls, heat spreaders, phase-change materials) is as important as evaluating the compute substrate. Ingress protection (IP ratings), MIL-STD-810 shock and vibration qualifications, and altitude derating curves all belong in the hardware evaluation dataset, not the safety section of the program review. Components that pass lab bench testing and fail in the field create program risk that is expensive to retire late in the acquisition cycle. Software Ecosystem and Toolchain Compatibility Hardware capability is only realizable if the software stack can exploit it. Evaluation must assess the compiler and runtime maturity for the target device: does the vendor's SDK support the model architecture in use (transformer blocks, custom operators, non-standard activation functions)? What operator coverage does the hardware-accelerated runtime provide, and what falls back to host CPU? How stable is the SDK across firmware releases? Toolchains that require proprietary model formats or impose conversion accuracy losses shift cost back onto the software team and may introduce latency from conversion overhead. The software evaluation runs in parallel with the hardware characterization; they are not sequential phases.

chunks.title: Tactical Edge AI Hardware Evaluation | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Supply Chain, Export Control, and Long-Term Availability
chunks.text: Supply Chain, Export Control, and Long-Term Availability The semiconductor supply chain is a national security consideration, not just a procurement detail. AI accelerators sourced from fabrication facilities subject to geopolitical disruption introduce program risk at sustainment. Export control classification of components affects what can be integrated into systems destined for allied partners or deployed internationally. Long-term availability commitments from vendors (production life, last-time-buy notices, form-factor stability) determine whether the hardware selection survives the program's full production run without costly re-qualification. Evaluating a module's country-of-origin for critical subsystems, and assessing vendor roadmaps for continuity, belongs in the hardware evaluation criteria alongside technical performance. Integration Profile and Platform Fit The selected accelerator module must fit the physical, electrical, and interface constraints of the target platform. Form factor standards (COM Express, VPX, SMARC, custom SOM) determine mechanical integration options and constrain board-level design choices. Interface bandwidth (PCIe lanes, USB throughput, MIPI CSI camera interfaces, Ethernet speeds) must support the sensor ingestion rates the mission requires without becoming the bottleneck. Power sequencing, voltage rail requirements, and boot time characteristics affect system integration complexity. Security features (secure boot, attestation, cryptographic accelerators, physical tamper detection) are increasingly required for programs operating under supply-chain risk management frameworks. Each of these integration dimensions is a gate, not a preference.

chunks.title: Edge Computing at Tactical Scale: Architecture Considerations | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Edge Computing at Tactical Scale: Architecture Considerations
chunks.text: Edge Computing at Tactical Scale: Architecture Considerations Insights Technical Publications Edge Computing at Tactical Scale A Ravonics architectural perspective on building compute for the environment you will actually operate in The tactical edge is not a smaller data center; it is a different design constraint entirely. Compute deployed forward must function in environments that are denied, degraded, intermittent, and limited (DDIL): bandwidth disappears, power is scarce, heat has nowhere to go, and the nearest rack is hundreds of miles away. The cloud-era assumptions of elastic capacity, always-on connectivity, and conditioned facilities simply do not hold. Architecting for these conditions means inverting the usual priorities. The following considerations outline how Ravonics approaches edge compute design: not as a checklist of products, but as a set of durable engineering principles for systems that must keep working when the network does not. Hardware Selection & SWaP Size, weight, and power (SWaP) drive every forward deployment. The right node balances compute density against what a vehicle, dismounted operator, or small platform can actually carry and power. Selection favors fanless, solid-state designs with documented operating envelopes over peak benchmark scores that assume rack cooling and shore power. Power & Thermal Budgets Every watt consumed is a watt that must be supplied and then dissipated. Design begins with a fixed power budget (battery, generator, or vehicle bus) and works backward to a thermal envelope the enclosure can shed without active cooling. Sustained workloads, not burst peaks, set the real ceiling for processing at the edge.

chunks.title: Edge Computing at Tactical Scale: Architecture Considerations | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Ruggedization & Environmental Resilience
chunks.text: Ruggedization & Environmental Resilience Field hardware faces shock, vibration, dust, moisture, and temperature swings that bench prototypes never see. Conformance to environmental and ingress standards is a baseline, not a finish line. Connectors, mounts, and cabling fail before silicon does, so resilience is engineered at the integration level, not bolted on afterward. Local-First Data & Storage When connectivity cannot be assumed, data must be captured, processed, and retained on the node itself. A local-first design treats the edge as the system of record between sync windows, with bounded storage, deliberate retention policies, and encryption at rest so that a captured or lost device does not become a disclosure event. Hybrid Edge-to-Cloud Overflow The edge handles what must happen now; the enterprise handles what can wait. A hybrid architecture defines clear boundaries for which workloads run forward and which overflow rearward, with sync that is opportunistic, prioritized, and tolerant of long gaps, reconciling state cleanly whenever a usable link returns, however briefly. Graceful Degradation & Autonomy A well-designed edge system does not fail when it is cut off; it degrades on purpose. Critical functions continue at reduced fidelity, non-essential features shed first, and the node keeps operating autonomously until reconnection. The operator is never left guessing whether the system is working or simply waiting on a network that is gone.

chunks.title: Federal Cloud Adoption: What FedRAMP-Aligned Architecture Actually Requires | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Federal Cloud Adoption: What FedRAMP-Aligned Architecture Actually Requires
chunks.text: Federal Cloud Adoption: What FedRAMP-Aligned Architecture Actually Requires Insights Industry Perspectives Federal Cloud & FedRAMP A Ravonics design-first perspective on FedRAMP-aligned cloud architecture, and an honest accounting of what the framework actually demands before an agency workload moves to the cloud Federal cloud adoption has accelerated since the 2017 Cloud Smart strategy and the OMB mandate requiring agencies to move workloads off legacy infrastructure. Yet the gap between "cloud-hosted" and "FedRAMP-authorized" remains wider than many program managers expect. The Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) is not a checkbox; it is a sustained engineering and governance commitment that begins at the architecture drawing board, not at the authorization package stage. Ravonics holds no FedRAMP authorization. What we bring is design-first architectural guidance: structuring cloud environments from the start so that the path to authorization (whether pursued by the agency's CSP or by the program itself) is navigable rather than remediated under deadline. The six considerations below reflect the structural choices that determine whether a cloud architecture is genuinely FedRAMP-aligned or simply cloud-hosted. Authorization Boundary Definition Every FedRAMP package begins with a precise authorization boundary: the documented scope of what is (and is not) covered by the security assessment. Agencies and cloud service providers routinely struggle here because modern cloud architectures blur the edges. Data flows traverse microservices, third-party APIs, and shared platform layers. Defining the boundary tightly enough to be assessable while broadly enough to cover the actual threat surface is the first and most consequential architectural decision. Boundary creep discovered late in the assessment cycle is among the most common causes of authorization delay.

chunks.title: Federal Cloud Adoption: What FedRAMP-Aligned Architecture Actually Requires | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Impact Level Selection (Low / Moderate / High, IL2-IL6)
chunks.text: Impact Level Selection (Low / Moderate / High, IL2-IL6) FedRAMP's impact levels (Low, Moderate, and High, mapped to DoW's IL2 through IL6 for defense workloads) determine the NIST SP 800-53 control baseline the system must satisfy. Most civilian agency workloads qualify for Moderate; defense workloads carrying CUI or mission-sensitive data may require High or IL4/IL5. Selecting the wrong level early forces either a costly re-architecture or an underpowered security posture. The decision should be driven by the data classification that will ever transit the system, not by what is convenient today. Control Inheritance and the Shared Responsibility Model FedRAMP's power is its inheritance model: an already-authorized CSP passes a defined set of controls downstream to agency tenants, reducing the assessment burden. But inheritance is not automatic; it must be explicitly documented, scoped to the specific service configuration in use, and verified against the CSP's current System Security Plan. Controls that are "inherited" in name but differ in implementation between the CSP's assessed environment and the agency's deployment create audit findings. Understanding exactly which controls are fully inherited, partially inherited, and fully agency-owned is foundational work that cannot be deferred. Continuous Monitoring (ConMon) Architecture FedRAMP authorization is not a one-time event. The Continuous Monitoring program requires monthly vulnerability scanning, annual penetration testing, Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) management, and regular reporting to the authorizing official. Agencies that design their cloud environments without instrumenting for ConMon from day one find themselves retrofitting logging pipelines, SIEM integrations, and scan tooling under operational pressure. Continuous monitoring should be a first-class design constraint alongside availability and cost, not an afterthought.

chunks.title: Federal Cloud Adoption: What FedRAMP-Aligned Architecture Actually Requires | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Identity, Access, and PIV/CAC Integration
chunks.text: Identity, Access, and PIV/CAC Integration Federal identity requirements do not relax in the cloud. HSPD-12, PIV/CAC authentication, and the phishing-resistant MFA requirements in OMB M-22-09 apply regardless of hosting environment. Cloud architectures that rely on username-and-password federation as a temporary measure routinely carry that debt into the authorization assessment. Building PIV/CAC-compatible identity providers, enforcing attribute-based access control, and logging every privileged session to a tamper-evident store are baseline expectations, not advanced features. Data Residency, Encryption, and Key Management Federal data at rest and in transit requires FIPS 140-2/140-3 validated cryptographic modules: a requirement that rules out default cloud encryption configurations that use non-validated libraries. Beyond algorithm selection, key management architecture determines who can compel access to federal data: the agency, the CSP, or both. Government-managed keys, hardware security module (HSM) integration, and explicit key custody documentation are standard expectations at Moderate and above. Agencies that deploy to the cloud without validating their cryptographic module chain against FIPS requirements discover the gap during the Third Party Assessment Organization (3PAO) assessment, not before. Want to discuss FedRAMP-aligned cloud architecture for your program? Ravonics provides design-first cloud architecture guidance to federal program managers and systems integrators building toward FedRAMP alignment. Whether you are scoping an authorization boundary, evaluating a CSP's inheritance model, or designing your continuous monitoring stack, we engage at the technical level. Ravonics holds no FedRAMP authorization; our value is helping programs get the architecture right from the start. Request a Conversation

chunks.title: Hyperspectral Imaging & Sensor Fusion | INSTAR Lab Research | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Hyperspectral Imaging & Sensor Fusion | INSTAR Lab Research
chunks.text: Hyperspectral Imaging & Sensor Fusion | INSTAR Lab Research Insights Research Directions Hyperspectral Sensor Fusion An overview of INSTAR Lab's physics-grounded research into hyperspectral imaging and multi-sensor fusion as a foundation for future SBIR/STTR development Conventional RGB cameras and even multispectral sensors capture a narrow slice of the electromagnetic spectrum. Hyperspectral imaging extends that coverage across dozens to hundreds of contiguous spectral bands, producing a three-dimensional data cube (two spatial dimensions and one spectral dimension) that encodes detailed material and compositional information invisible to broadband sensors. That richness creates opportunities for object classification, camouflage penetration, anomaly detection, and material identification that cannot be achieved through spatial or intensity cues alone. For defense and intelligence sensing applications, those capabilities have long been a research priority; the challenge has been making them fast, compact, and interpretable enough for operational use. INSTAR Lab, a Ravonics partner and the 501(c)(3) R&D bench in the ecosystem, is exploring hyperspectral imaging as one of its active physics research directions. The bench, led by Dr. Spoogmay Khan (PhD Physics, Material Sciences), is examining the intersection of physics-informed spectral modeling, deep learning, and multi-sensor fusion. This research direction is exploratory and targets future SBIR/STTR opportunities; no fielded system or program of record currently exists. The pillars below describe the technical landscape the bench is working within.

chunks.title: Hyperspectral Imaging & Sensor Fusion | INSTAR Lab Research | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Spectral Data Cube Acquisition and Processing
chunks.text: Spectral Data Cube Acquisition and Processing Hyperspectral sensors generate large, high-dimensional data volumes. A modest airborne pushbroom imager scanning at 200 spectral bands produces an order of magnitude more raw data per frame than a comparable RGB camera. Efficient acquisition pipelines must address on-sensor data reduction, calibration (radiometric, atmospheric, and geometric), and band selection to limit the dimensionality forwarded to classification models. Research interest lies in whether learned spectral encoders can adaptively compress the cube in a way that preserves the discriminative features most relevant to the downstream detection task, rather than applying fixed band subsets. Deep Learning for Spectral Classification Classical hyperspectral classification relied on support vector machines and hand-crafted spectral libraries. Deep learning has substantially advanced the field: convolutional networks applied across spatial-spectral patches, recurrent architectures that treat spectral bands as a sequence, and transformer-based models that attend across both spatial and spectral dimensions have each demonstrated competitive performance on benchmark datasets. The research question INSTAR Lab is investigating is how well these models generalize when spectral libraries shift due to sensor aging, environmental conditions, or sensor substitution: a practical concern for any deployed system that must operate reliably over time rather than only on the training distribution.

chunks.title: Hyperspectral Imaging & Sensor Fusion | INSTAR Lab Research | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Physics-Informed Spectral Modeling
chunks.text: Physics-Informed Spectral Modeling The physics of light-matter interaction constrains what spectral signatures are physically realizable. Physics-informed neural networks and radiative-transfer-aware architectures embed those constraints as inductive biases, reducing the labeled data required to achieve reliable classification and improving robustness when operational conditions differ from training conditions. For material sciences researchers on the bench, the connection between measured spectral reflectance and underlying material composition is a natural bridge between physics domain knowledge and machine learning. This modeling approach also supports synthetic data generation for rare or sensitive material classes where labeled real-world examples are scarce. Multi-Sensor Fusion Architecture No single sensor modality is sufficient for robust object detection and classification in contested environments. Hyperspectral data provides spectral richness but is challenged by lighting conditions and spatial resolution limits. LiDAR provides precise 3D geometry but no material information. Synthetic aperture radar penetrates foliage and weather but requires specialized interpretation. Fusing complementary modalities at the feature level (rather than simply stacking outputs) allows a unified model to exploit the strengths of each while compensating for individual sensor failures or adversarial masking. Architecture choices for fusion (early, intermediate, or late; learned weighting vs fixed combination) depend strongly on the synchronization properties and relative reliability of the input streams.

chunks.title: Hyperspectral Imaging & Sensor Fusion | INSTAR Lab Research | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Edge-Deployable Inference for Hyperspectral Models
chunks.text: Edge-Deployable Inference for Hyperspectral Models Operational sensing systems often cannot relay full hyperspectral cubes to a remote compute node for classification; latency, bandwidth, and connectivity constraints push inference toward the sensor or the platform. Running deep hyperspectral models on SWaP-constrained edge hardware requires the same optimization disciplines (quantization, pruning, knowledge distillation) that apply to other large models, but with the added complication that spectral data pipelines are not yet as well supported by edge-AI frameworks as standard image formats. Research into lightweight spectral backbone architectures, on-sensor spectral compression, and efficient inference runtimes is a necessary complement to the classification model work. Anomaly Detection and Change Detection Beyond target classification, hyperspectral imagery enables statistical anomaly detection: identifying pixels or regions whose spectral signature deviates from the local background without requiring a predefined target class. This is valuable for detecting novel or unknown materials, identifying recent disturbances in a scene, and supporting wide-area surveillance tasks where exhaustive labeling of all potential targets is not feasible. Change detection across temporally separated hyperspectral acquisitions of the same area can reveal concealment, construction, or activity patterns that are invisible in single-epoch imagery. INSTAR Lab's physics background informs interpretation of what those statistical anomalies represent at the material level.

chunks.title: JADC2 Integration: Multi-Domain C2 Architecture Patterns | Ravonics
chunks.heading: JADC2 Integration: Multi-Domain C2 Architecture Patterns
chunks.text: JADC2 Integration: Multi-Domain C2 Architecture Patterns Insights Technical Publications JADC2 Integration A Ravonics perspective on why interoperability (not any single platform) is the hard problem in multi-domain operations JADC2 sets out to connect sensors and decision-makers across every operational domain (air, land, sea, space, and cyber) so that the right data reaches the right node at the speed of relevance. The vision is not a new radio or a new application; it is a network of networks in which any sensor can inform any effect, regardless of which service, program, or vendor fielded it. Our thesis is that the hard problem is not any one platform; it is interoperability and data. Connecting heterogeneous systems that were never designed to talk to one another, reconciling their data models, and moving information across accreditation boundaries is where multi-domain integration succeeds or fails. New entrants add value precisely by being integration-disciplined and standards-first rather than by fielding yet another stovepipe to be bridged later. Data-Centric Architecture Decouple data from the applications that produce and consume it. When information lives in a shared, addressable data layer rather than locked inside point solutions, new capabilities subscribe to what already exists instead of demanding bespoke integrations. This inverts the traditional application-centric model and is the structural prerequisite for any sensor informing any effect across a federation of systems.

chunks.title: JADC2 Integration: Multi-Domain C2 Architecture Patterns | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Open Standards & Common Data Models
chunks.text: Open Standards & Common Data Models Interoperability at scale depends on published, vendor-neutral interfaces and shared data models, not proprietary connectors negotiated one pair at a time. Adopting open message formats, common schemas, and documented APIs lets independently developed systems exchange information without custom glue. Standards-first design also protects the program from lock-in and keeps the integration surface auditable over a long acquisition lifecycle. Semantic Interoperability A shared format is necessary but not sufficient; systems must also share meaning. A track, a unit, or a time reference has to carry the same definition across every participating system, or fused pictures quietly diverge. Ontologies, controlled vocabularies, and explicit unit and reference conventions give data unambiguous interpretation, so that machines, not just operators, can reason over information that crossed a domain boundary. Event-Driven Mesh & Publish/Subscribe Multi-domain C2 favors loosely coupled, event-driven messaging over brittle request/response chains. A publish/subscribe mesh lets producers emit information once and any authorized consumer react, with no producer needing to know its consumers in advance. This pattern scales as nodes join and leave, tolerates partial connectivity, and keeps the architecture open to capabilities that were not anticipated when the system was first fielded. Cross-Domain & Multi-Level Security Moving data between networks of different sensitivity requires deliberate, accredited separation rather than ad hoc bridges. One-way data guards, controlled interfaces, and clear accreditation boundaries let information flow where policy permits while enforcing the direction and content of every transfer. The design goal is principled data movement that respects security boundaries by construction, not by exception, and never by assumption.

chunks.title: JADC2 Integration: Multi-Domain C2 Architecture Patterns | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Test, Observability & Graceful Degradation
chunks.text: Test, Observability & Graceful Degradation A federation is only as trustworthy as its weakest link, so integration must be continuously tested and instrumented end to end. Contract testing, distributed tracing, and health telemetry across federated systems surface faults before an operator does. Just as important is graceful degradation: when a node, link, or feed drops, the wider picture should narrow predictably rather than fail outright, preserving usable command and control under stress. Want to discuss JADC2 integration for your program? Ravonics is built to help federal program managers and systems integrators translate these architectural principles into acquisition-ready solutions. Whether you are scoping an IDIQ task order, evaluating a COTS AI platform, or designing a new edge compute stack, we engage at the technical level. chunks.title: JADC2 Multi-Domain Integration: Why Interoperability Is the Hard Problem | Ravonics
chunks.heading: JADC2 Multi-Domain Integration: Why Interoperability Is the Hard Problem
chunks.text: JADC2 Multi-Domain Integration: Why Interoperability Is the Hard Problem Insights Industry Perspectives JADC2 Interoperability A Ravonics industry perspective on why JADC2's defining challenge is semantic interoperability across service silos (not bandwidth or processing speed) Joint All-Domain Command and Control is the defining C2 modernization program of the current defense era, and the ambition is genuinely transformative: sense, make sense, and act across land, sea, air, space, and cyberspace faster than any adversary can respond. The program has attracted substantial investment, generated a crowded ecosystem of data-link and cloud-native integration proposals, and produced important technical work at each service's program office. Yet the hardest problem remains stubbornly unsolved, and it is not the one most vendors are selling solutions to. Bandwidth, latency, and compute power are real constraints, but they are tractable engineering problems with established solution patterns. The constraint that actually determines whether JADC2 produces a coherent joint picture or a cacophony of incompatible service feeds is semantic interoperability: whether a track generated by a Navy sensor and a target record produced by an Air Force ISR platform mean the same thing when they arrive at a joint C2 node. Without a shared data model, all the transport capacity in the world delivers unresolvable ambiguity at the decision layer. The following perspective examines the six strategic dimensions that separate programs that achieve genuine multi-domain fusion from those that produce integration theater.

chunks.title: JADC2 Multi-Domain Integration: Why Interoperability Is the Hard Problem | Ravonics
chunks.heading: The Semantic Gap Is the Core Problem
chunks.text: The Semantic Gap Is the Core Problem Each military service has evolved its own data models, message formats, and ontologies over decades of independent system development. A "track" in one service's lexicon carries different mandatory fields, confidence scoring, and provenance metadata than a nominally equivalent record in another's. When these heterogeneous feeds arrive at a joint fusion engine, the system faces a choice: force a lowest-common-denominator schema that loses critical context, or maintain parallel representations that defeat the purpose of fusion. Neither outcome is acceptable at the speed multi-domain operations demand. Closing the semantic gap requires agreement on a common data model (not a translation layer, but a shared meaning layer) that each domain's data is mapped into before it enters the joint fabric. Data Fabric Architecture Over Point-to-Point Integration The instinct of many integration programs is to build bilateral connectors: translate System A's output into System B's input. This approach scales as O(n²): each new node added to the joint network requires new connectors to every existing node. A data fabric architecture inverts this: each system publishes to and subscribes from a shared semantic layer governed by common schemas and access policies. New participants write one adapter to the fabric, not dozens of bilateral integrations. The architectural choice between connector sprawl and a fabric model is a program-level strategic decision that determines long-term maintainability and the cost of adding new joint partners.

chunks.title: JADC2 Multi-Domain Integration: Why Interoperability Is the Hard Problem | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Standards Adoption Is a Policy Problem, Not a Technical One
chunks.text: Standards Adoption Is a Policy Problem, Not a Technical One Common data model standards for defense (NATO STANAG 5516, USMTF, emerging JADC2 data standards from CDAO) exist or are in active development. The technical content is generally sound. The barrier to adoption is not schema quality; it is service-level program sovereignty. Each service's program office controls its own acquisition budget and schedule, and conforming to a joint standard imposes cost and schedule risk that falls on one program while the benefit accrues jointly. Resolving this requires acquisition policy mechanisms: contract data requirements lists that mandate schema conformance, DoW Chief Digital and AI Office (CDAO) governance with enforcement authority, and joint requirements that make interoperability a first-class acceptance criterion rather than an integration test afterthought. Cross-Domain Security Is a First-Order Architectural Constraint Multi-domain C2 necessarily spans classification boundaries. A joint common operational picture that fuses intelligence community feeds with unclassified partner-nation data must enforce access control at the attribute level, not just at the network perimeter. Cross-domain solutions (CDS) that guard data flows between classification enclaves introduce latency, impose schema constraints, and create single points of failure. Architects who treat cross-domain security as an afterthought (a gateway to bolt on once the fusion architecture is designed) consistently discover that the CDS requirements reshape the entire data model. Cross-domain policy must inform schema design from the beginning, not be retrofitted to an architecture that assumed a single-domain world.

chunks.title: JADC2 Multi-Domain Integration: Why Interoperability Is the Hard Problem | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Disconnected and Degraded Operations Require Edge Coherence
chunks.text: Disconnected and Degraded Operations Require Edge Coherence JADC2's vision of a continuously fused joint picture assumes some level of connectivity. Real multi-domain operations include periods of denied, degraded, intermittent, and limited (DDIL) communications where individual nodes lose access to the joint fabric entirely. The interoperability architecture must define behavior during disconnected operations: what local state is authoritative, how conflicts are resolved on reconnect, and what minimum data set a node needs to operate autonomously. Programs that design only for the connected case build a system that degrades gracefully in the lab and catastrophically in the field. Edge coherence is an interoperability requirement, not a communications requirement. Measuring Interoperability Requires Joint Test Events Interoperability cannot be self-certified. A service that tests its JADC2 interface against its own message simulator is measuring compliance with its own assumptions, not actual joint compatibility. The only credible measure is a joint test event where heterogeneous systems operated by different organizations exchange live data under realistic mission scenarios and adjudicate disagreements at the schema level, not at the "it worked in the demo" level. Programs that reach this standard expose the semantic gaps early, when they are fixable. Programs that defer joint testing until late-stage integration typically surface incompatibilities that are expensive to fix and politically difficult to acknowledge. Genuine interoperability is demonstrated in adversarial joint exercises, not vendor showcases.

chunks.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography: Preparing Federal Communications | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Post-Quantum Cryptography: Preparing Federal Communications
chunks.text: Post-Quantum Cryptography: Preparing Federal Communications Insights Technical Publications Post-Quantum Cryptography A Ravonics architectural primer on protecting today's secrets against tomorrow's quantum adversary The public-key cryptography securing federal communications today rests on mathematical problems that classical computers cannot solve in any practical time. A sufficiently capable quantum computer changes that calculus: Shor's algorithm would break the RSA and elliptic-curve schemes underpinning TLS, VPNs, code signing, and key exchange across nearly every federal system. The timeline for such a machine remains uncertain, but the risk window has already opened. The reason is a threat model called "harvest now, decrypt later." A capable adversary does not need a quantum computer today to benefit from one tomorrow. They need only to capture encrypted traffic now and store it. When a cryptographically relevant quantum computer arrives, that archived traffic is retroactively exposed. For federal communications (diplomatic cables, intelligence reporting, classified program data, and personnel records with decades-long sensitivity) the secret you transmit today may still demand protection long after quantum decryption becomes feasible. That mismatch is why the migration must begin now, not when the threat fully materializes. The Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later Threat Adversaries are already recording encrypted federal traffic and archiving it against a future decryption capability. The governing question is not when a quantum computer arrives, but how long your data must stay secret. Where that lifetime exceeds the migration window plus the adversary's likely time-to-capability, the secret is effectively at risk today, and waiting only widens the exposure.

chunks.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography: Preparing Federal Communications | Ravonics
chunks.heading: The New NIST Standards
chunks.text: The New NIST Standards In 2024 NIST finalized its first post-quantum standards: FIPS 203 specifies ML-KEM (formerly Kyber) for key encapsulation, FIPS 204 specifies ML-DSA (formerly Dilithium) for digital signatures, and FIPS 205 specifies SLH-DSA (formerly SPHINCS+), a stateless hash-based signature with conservative security assumptions. These lattice- and hash-based schemes resist known quantum attacks and form the foundation for compliant federal migration. Cryptographic Inventory & Dependency Mapping You cannot migrate what you cannot see. The first practical step is a thorough inventory of every place cryptography lives: protocols, libraries, certificates, hardware modules, embedded firmware, and third-party services. Mapping these dependencies surfaces hidden uses, quantifies data sensitivity and lifetime, and produces the prioritized, risk-ranked basis for any credible transition plan. Cryptographic Agility Hard-coding a single algorithm is what made the current transition so painful. Cryptographic agility abstracts algorithms behind stable interfaces, so primitives can be swapped through configuration and policy rather than re-engineering. Designing for agility now means the next standard (or an emergency response to a broken scheme) becomes a managed change rather than a multi-year forklift across the enterprise. Hybrid / Phased Transition Federal migration favors hybrid schemes that run a classical algorithm and a post-quantum algorithm in parallel, combining both into a single key exchange. The session stays secure as long as either holds, hedging against an immature PQC implementation while delivering quantum resistance immediately. A phased rollout (beginning with the highest-sensitivity, longest-lived channels) contains risk and builds operational confidence.

chunks.text: Governance, Testing & Roadmap Alignment Migration is a governance program, not a one-time patch. Align planning with NSA's CNSA 2.0 timelines and federal guidance, establish interoperability and regression testing for hybrid stacks, and validate against the standardized parameter sets. Clear ownership, measurable milestones, and a maintained roadmap keep the effort on track as standards mature and agency mandates take effect. Want to discuss post-quantum readiness for your program?
