chunks.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Architecture for Federal Systems | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Post-Quantum Cryptography Architecture for Federal Systems
chunks.text: Post-Quantum Cryptography Architecture for Federal Systems Insights Research Directions PQC Federal Architecture A Ravonics implementation architecture perspective on deploying NIST-standardized post-quantum algorithms across federal communications and data-at-rest The National Institute of Standards and Technology finalized its first post-quantum cryptography standards in 2024: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM, the key encapsulation mechanism based on CRYSTALS-Kyber), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA, the digital signature scheme based on CRYSTALS-Dilithium), and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, a stateless hash-based signature alternative). For federal agencies and defense contractors, these publications shift the conversation from "should we prepare?" to "how do we build systems that actually implement these algorithms correctly, safely, and at scale?" The threat framing (harvest-now-decrypt-later, CRQC timeline uncertainty) is well established. What deserves focused attention now is the engineering architecture required to make PQC migration tractable. Federal cryptographic infrastructure spans an enormous surface: TLS sessions, VPN tunnels, code-signing pipelines, PKI hierarchies, data-at-rest encryption, hardware security modules, and embedded firmware across platforms and classification levels. Each of these has different upgrade cycles, different key-lifecycle constraints, and different tolerance for latency or bandwidth overhead. A successful PQC migration is not a library swap; it is a sequenced architectural program that must be planned and executed with care. The sections below outline the implementation architecture pillars Ravonics applies when assessing this challenge for federal programs.

chunks.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Architecture for Federal Systems | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Crypto-Agility by Design
chunks.text: Crypto-Agility by Design Crypto-agility is the property that lets a system negotiate, swap, or upgrade its cryptographic algorithms without requiring a full re-architecture of the surrounding application. Achieving it means abstracting algorithm selection behind well-defined interfaces (a key encapsulation provider, a signature provider) so that substituting ML-KEM for ECDH, or ML-DSA for ECDSA, requires changing a configuration and a library binding, not rewriting protocol handlers. Systems that hardcode algorithm identifiers into wire formats or database schemas sacrifice agility. Federal programs with long acquisition and sustainment timelines should treat crypto-agility as a first-class architectural requirement, not a retrofit, because the algorithm landscape will continue to evolve as cryptanalysis matures. Hybrid Classical + PQC Modes Until ML-KEM and ML-DSA accumulate a longer field history, the recommended transition posture for high-assurance federal use is a hybrid mode: combining a classical algorithm (e.g., ECDH P-384 or X25519) with its PQC counterpart in a single key agreement, so that security is maintained if either primitive is broken. NSA's CNSA 2.0 guidance and IETF drafts for hybrid TLS and SSH both reflect this approach. The architectural implication is that protocol stacks must support composite key material (larger handshake payloads and more complex key derivation) while preserving interoperability with endpoints that cannot yet negotiate PQC. Graceful fallback logic and clear minimum-version policy are necessary to avoid silent downgrade.

chunks.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Architecture for Federal Systems | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Key Management Infrastructure
chunks.text: Key Management Infrastructure ML-KEM and ML-DSA keys differ materially from their classical predecessors in size: ML-KEM-768 public keys are 1,184 bytes, ML-DSA-65 public keys are 1,952 bytes, and signatures are correspondingly larger. Key management systems (certificate authorities, HSMs, PKI directories, key vaults) must be assessed for whether they can store, distribute, and validate keys and signatures at these sizes within existing bandwidth and storage budgets. Hardware security modules require firmware or replacement if they do not support the new algorithms natively. PKI hierarchies that issue long-lived certificates must plan for re-issuance windows that align with certificate lifetimes and mission operational calendars. Cryptographic Inventory and Asset Mapping Migration sequencing requires knowing precisely where classical public-key cryptography lives across the enterprise. An effective cryptographic inventory catalogs every system, protocol, library version, and data store that relies on RSA, ECDSA, ECDH, or Diffie-Hellman for confidentiality or integrity. Automated scanning tools can surface many uses, but embedded firmware and legacy middleware often require manual review. The inventory output (an asset map with algorithm, key length, certificate authority, and renewal cycle) becomes the migration backlog and the basis for risk-tiered sequencing. High-sensitivity data channels and long-retention encrypted archives should be prioritized; internal low-sensitivity services can follow on a slower schedule.

chunks.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Architecture for Federal Systems | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Phased Migration Sequencing
chunks.text: Phased Migration Sequencing Attempting a simultaneous enterprise-wide cutover to PQC is not realistic for federal programs. A phased sequence (typically new internet-facing TLS endpoints first, then internal PKI, then VPN and remote-access infrastructure, then application-layer signing, then data-at-rest re-encryption) allows teams to gain operational confidence with each algorithm in low-risk contexts before applying it to high-consequence channels. Phases should be gated: each phase requires proof of HSM support, interoperability testing against partner systems, and rollback capability before proceeding. OMB and NSM-10 guidance provide policy timelines; program offices should map those timelines against their own asset inventory to produce a credible sequenced plan. Performance and Overhead Characterization PQC algorithms carry meaningful performance differences relative to classical counterparts. ML-KEM is computationally efficient; SLH-DSA signing is significantly slower than RSA or ECDSA. Latency-sensitive protocols (mutual TLS handshakes under tight SLA, firmware update signing chains, real-time command authentication) must be benchmarked with actual PQC implementations on representative hardware before deployment. Embedded and resource-constrained endpoints (tactical radios, sensor nodes, embedded controllers) may require hardware acceleration or algorithm-level parameter choices that balance security and performance within platform constraints. Characterizing overhead early prevents surprises at integration and test. Governance, Testing, and Validation PQC migration is a program-level governance event, not a library update ticket. It requires change control integration, formal interoperability testing against NIST test vectors and partner implementations, security assessment under RMF or equivalent authority-to-operate processes, and continuous monitoring to detect algorithm misconfiguration or downgrade. Automated regression testing should verify that hybrid modes are being exercised (not silently bypassed) and that key sizes and signature parameters match the selected FIPS standard. For programs subject to CNSS or IC policy, coordination with accreditation authorities early in the design phase avoids rework at ATO time.

chunks.title: Quantum Computing for Defense Optimization | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Quantum Computing for Defense Optimization
chunks.text: Quantum Computing for Defense Optimization Insights Research Directions Quantum Defense Optimization An INSTAR Lab research direction: applying quantum optimization algorithms to the combinatorial scheduling, routing, and tasking problems that classical solvers find intractable at mission scale Defense planning confronts a class of problems that scales combinatorially: assigning sensor assets across a theater, sequencing logistics convoys through contested routes, scheduling maintenance windows across a distributed fleet, or allocating electromagnetic spectrum in a congested environment. Classical algorithms handle modest versions of these problems well, but operational scale (hundreds of assets, thousands of constraints, compressed time windows) drives solution times beyond what tactical decision cycles permit. Heuristics help, but they trade optimality for speed in ways that may matter when margins are tight. Quantum computing offers a structurally different approach to this problem class. Rather than searching solution spaces sequentially, quantum algorithms exploit superposition and interference to evaluate multiple candidate solutions simultaneously. Current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware is still far from fault-tolerant at the scale needed for live operational use, but the research trajectory is clear, and the window for establishing foundational competency is now. INSTAR Lab (Ravonics' affiliated 501(c)(3) research bench) is pursuing this as a research direction targeting future SBIR/STTR engagement, not a shipping product. The sections below describe the conceptual pillars shaping that inquiry.

chunks.title: Quantum Computing for Defense Optimization | Ravonics
chunks.heading: The Defense Optimization Problem Class
chunks.text: The Defense Optimization Problem Class The problems of interest are combinatorial: they involve selecting, ordering, or assigning discrete items under constraints, with an exponentially large solution space. Canonical forms include vehicle routing problems, traveling-salesman variants, quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO), and constraint-satisfaction problems. Defense instantiations include multi-UAV waypoint planning, ISR sensor retasking, supply route deconfliction, and communications frequency assignment. Each shares the property that classical exact solvers become intractable as instance size grows, making them natural targets for quantum speedup research. Gate-Model vs. Quantum Annealing Approaches Two hardware paradigms are relevant. Gate-model quantum computers (IBM, Google, IonQ) execute sequences of quantum logic gates on qubits: general-purpose, but currently limited to shallow circuits by noise. Quantum annealers (D-Wave) are purpose-built for QUBO problems, mapping the cost function directly onto physical qubit couplings and allowing the system to relax toward a minimum-energy configuration. Annealers can handle larger instances today on their native problem class, but gate models promise broader applicability as hardware matures. INSTAR Lab's research evaluates both paradigms against defense-relevant problem encodings. Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) QAOA is the leading candidate gate-model algorithm for combinatorial optimization on near-term hardware. It encodes the optimization objective as a cost Hamiltonian and applies alternating cost and mixer unitaries, parameterized by angles that are classically tuned to steer the quantum state toward good solutions. Depth (number of rounds, denoted p) trades circuit complexity against solution quality; shallow circuits are NISQ-feasible but yield approximate results. Understanding where QAOA outperforms classical approximation algorithms, and for which problem structures, is a key open question in the research community and a focal point for INSTAR Lab's benchmarking work.

chunks.title: Quantum Computing for Defense Optimization | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Hybrid Classical-Quantum Architectures
chunks.text: Hybrid Classical-Quantum Architectures Full quantum solutions to large defense problems are not feasible on near-term hardware. The practical near-term model is hybrid: classical processors handle problem decomposition, parameter optimization, and result post-processing, while the quantum processor is invoked for the computationally intensive subproblem where quantum advantage is expected to emerge. Variational quantum eigensolvers and quantum-classical feedback loops exemplify this pattern. Designing effective decompositions (knowing which subproblems benefit from quantum treatment and which are better left classical) is itself a research contribution that defense-domain expertise informs directly. NISQ Realism and Error Considerations Current quantum hardware is noisy: gate errors, decoherence, and readout errors accumulate with circuit depth, degrading result quality. NISQ-era research must account for this honestly. Error mitigation techniques (zero-noise extrapolation, probabilistic error cancellation, symmetry verification) extend the useful depth of near-term circuits but add classical overhead. Fault-tolerant quantum computing, which would enable deep circuits and strong guarantees, requires logical qubits built from many physical qubits and remains a medium-to-long horizon. INSTAR Lab's research posture acknowledges these constraints and targets problem formulations and circuit depths appropriate to demonstrated hardware capability. Near-Term vs. Long-Term Research Horizon Near-term work focuses on problem encoding, benchmark development, and hybrid architecture design: contributions that accrue regardless of when fault-tolerant hardware arrives and position the team to exploit improved hardware as it becomes available. Medium-term milestones include demonstrating quantum advantage on small, defense-relevant benchmark instances. Long-term, fault-tolerant hardware opens the door to Grover-style unstructured search and quantum speedups on constraint-satisfaction problems at operationally relevant scale. Ravonics and INSTAR Lab are building toward this trajectory through SBIR/STTR research pathways, not claiming current product capability.

chunks.title: The Quantum Threat: Why Federal Systems Should Begin PQC Migration Now | Ravonics
chunks.heading: The Quantum Threat: Why Federal Systems Should Begin PQC Migration Now
chunks.text: The Quantum Threat: Why Federal Systems Should Begin PQC Migration Now Insights Industry Perspectives Quantum Threat & PQC A Ravonics perspective on the harvest-now-decrypt-later threat, CRQC timeline uncertainty, and why the policy signal from NIST, NSA, and OMB points clearly toward beginning post-quantum migration before a quantum computer arrives No cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) exists today. Estimates for when one might arrive range from a decade to several decades, and experts disagree sharply. That uncertainty is precisely the problem. The primary threat to federal cryptographic infrastructure is not a quantum computer that breaks encryption on the day it is switched on. The threat is adversaries collecting encrypted federal data right now, archiving it, and waiting until the compute capability to decrypt it becomes available. This is the harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL) model, and it converts timeline uncertainty from a reason to wait into a reason to act. The policy signal from the federal government has been unambiguous. National Security Memorandum 10 (NSM-10, 2022) directed agencies to inventory cryptographic systems and prioritize migration to quantum-resistant algorithms. NIST finalized three post-quantum cryptography standards in 2024: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM, key encapsulation), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA, digital signatures), and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, stateless hash-based signatures). NSA's Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 2.0 (CNSA 2.0) establishes transition timelines for National Security Systems, with deadlines that are already in progress. The question for federal programs is not whether to migrate; it is how to begin.

chunks.title: The Quantum Threat: Why Federal Systems Should Begin PQC Migration Now | Ravonics
chunks.heading: The Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later Threat Model
chunks.text: The Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later Threat Model HNDL requires no quantum computer today. A sophisticated adversary needs only the ability to intercept and store ciphertext: a capability that state-level actors demonstrably possess. Data with long-term sensitivity (treaty negotiations, intelligence sources and methods, classified R&D, long-lived identity credentials) encrypted under RSA-2048 or ECC P-256 today will be vulnerable the moment a CRQC becomes available. The asymmetry is stark: the cost to harvest is low and immediate; the cost to retroactively protect data that has already been collected is zero on the adversary's side. Programs that handle data whose sensitivity must survive beyond a 10-15 year horizon cannot treat CRQC timelines as someone else's problem. CRQC Timeline Uncertainty Argues for Earlier Action Expert consensus places a fault-tolerant CRQC capable of running Shor's algorithm against RSA-2048 somewhere in the range of 10 to 30 years out, with significant variance in both directions. But migration is not instantaneous. Federal programs operate on multi-year acquisition and fielding cycles. Cryptographic libraries are embedded in firmware, hardware security modules, PKI infrastructure, and protocols that take years to update across a large installed base. A 15-year CRQC estimate combined with a 10-year migration cycle leaves very little margin. Starting when the threat is confirmed leaves no margin at all.

chunks.title: The Quantum Threat: Why Federal Systems Should Begin PQC Migration Now | Ravonics
chunks.heading: NIST FIPS 203, 204, and 205: The Standardized Algorithms
chunks.text: NIST FIPS 203, 204, and 205: The Standardized Algorithms After an eight-year standardization process, NIST finalized three post-quantum algorithms in August 2024. ML-KEM (FIPS 203, based on CRYSTALS-Kyber) covers key encapsulation for key exchange and hybrid encryption. ML-DSA (FIPS 204, based on CRYSTALS-Dilithium) covers general-purpose digital signatures. SLH-DSA (FIPS 205, based on SPHINCS+) provides a hash-based signature alternative with different security assumptions and performance tradeoffs. These are not experimental candidates; they are published federal standards with FIPS validation on the roadmap. Agency programs should begin evaluating library support and planning integration sequencing now. NSA CNSA 2.0 and National Security System Timelines NSA's CNSA 2.0 guidance, published in 2022, establishes specific transition timelines for the National Security System (NSS) community. Software and firmware applications are expected to support CNSA 2.0 algorithms by 2025 and exclusively use them by 2030. Networking equipment, operating systems, and hardware face staggered deadlines extending to 2033. These are not aspirational targets; they are program office obligations for NSS owners. Defense contractors and systems integrators supporting NSS programs need to understand where their delivered products fall in the CNSA 2.0 timeline and plan accordingly. NSM-10, OMB, and the Cryptographic Inventory Requirement NSM-10 directed agencies to produce a prioritized inventory of cryptographic systems by mid-2023, with particular attention to systems that protect data with long-term sensitivity. OMB followed with implementation guidance reinforcing the inventory requirement and tying it to existing FISMA reporting processes. The inventory is not the endpoint; it is the precondition for every subsequent migration decision. Programs that have not yet mapped which protocols, libraries, certificates, and key exchange mechanisms they use cannot sequence a migration, identify dependencies, or estimate cost. The inventory must come first.

chunks.title: The Quantum Threat: Why Federal Systems Should Begin PQC Migration Now | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Crypto-Agility as the Migration Strategy
chunks.text: Crypto-Agility as the Migration Strategy The practical migration approach most aligned with federal program realities is crypto-agility: designing systems to support algorithm negotiation and replacement without architectural rewrites. Hybrid classical-plus-PQC modes (combining, for example, X25519 with ML-KEM in a single key exchange) allow programs to maintain classical security during the transition while gaining quantum resistance, without betting everything on a single algorithm family before broader operational experience accumulates. Building agility in now means future algorithm updates become configuration and library changes rather than re-architecture. Programs that bake in specific algorithms at the protocol level today will pay a far higher migration cost when the mandate arrives. Want to discuss quantum-threat posture and PQC planning for your program? Ravonics is built to help federal program managers and systems integrators translate NSM-10, NIST FIPS 203/204/205, and CNSA 2.0 requirements into actionable migration planning. Whether you are starting a cryptographic inventory, evaluating hybrid PQC modes, or assessing where your systems fall on the CNSA 2.0 timeline, we engage at the technical level. chunks.title: Autonomous Swarm Coordination | Architecture Concepts | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Autonomous Swarm Coordination | Architecture Concepts
chunks.text: Autonomous Swarm Coordination | Architecture Concepts Insights Research Directions Swarm Coordination Concepts A Ravonics architectural perspective on the coordination patterns, consensus mechanisms, and degraded-environment behaviors that determine whether a multi-platform autonomous formation holds together when the network does not Fielding a single autonomous platform is a tractable engineering problem. Fielding a coordinated formation of autonomous platforms (each making local decisions, each affecting the others) is a fundamentally different class of challenge. The value of a swarm is collective: coverage no single platform could achieve, redundancy that survives attrition, parallelism that compresses timelines. But collective behavior requires coordination, and coordination requires assumptions about communication that contested environments actively work to defeat. GPS can be jammed. Datalinks can be denied. Nodes can be lost mid-mission. The architecture must account for these conditions as design inputs, not edge cases. The sections below examine the architectural concepts Ravonics considers when evaluating or advising on multi-platform autonomy programs. This is not a description of a deployed Ravonics product; it is a structured view of the design space, informed by the partner-ecosystem autonomy software Ravonics bridges to federal acquisition, and by the systems-engineering principles that govern how these platforms are evaluated, integrated, and sustained within federal programs.

chunks.title: Autonomous Swarm Coordination | Architecture Concepts | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Decentralized vs. Hierarchical Control
chunks.text: Decentralized vs. Hierarchical Control A fully centralized swarm controller is a single point of failure: lose the controller node, and formation coherence collapses. Decentralized architectures distribute authority across agents: each platform maintains a local world model and makes binding decisions from it, coordinating with neighbors rather than awaiting direction from above. Pure decentralization maximizes resilience but introduces consistency challenges: agents may hold divergent state views, producing conflicting actions. Hierarchical hybrid designs (local reactive control, peer-layer coordination, and optional higher-level intent injection) balance resilience and coherence. The right decomposition depends on mission tempo, expected communication availability, and the criticality of synchronized action. Consensus and Distributed State Agreement For platforms to act in concert, they must agree on shared facts: current formation geometry, task assignments, which targets are already engaged, which zones are denied. Consensus protocols (drawn from distributed systems theory) allow a network of agents to converge on a shared value despite unreliable links and node failures. Byzantine-fault-tolerant variants handle adversarial conditions where some nodes may be compromised or spoofed. Defense applications add the constraint that consensus must complete within mission-relevant time windows, not the seconds tolerated in enterprise systems. Gossip protocols, leader-election mechanisms, and conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) each offer different trade-offs between convergence speed, bandwidth consumption, and robustness to partition.

chunks.title: Autonomous Swarm Coordination | Architecture Concepts | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Resilient Positioning, Navigation, and Timing (PNT)
chunks.text: Resilient Positioning, Navigation, and Timing (PNT) GPS denial removes the shared time and position reference that most coordination protocols implicitly assume. Resilient PNT architectures layer multiple positioning sources: inertial navigation (with bounded drift), terrain-relative navigation, visual odometry, ranging between platforms, and opportunistic use of non-GPS signals. Time synchronization shifts to disciplined oscillators, PTP over mesh links, or platform-to-platform pulse exchange. Each source has accuracy, latency, and fault characteristics that must be characterized and fused. The architecture must define graceful degradation: what coordination behaviors remain valid as PNT confidence degrades, and at what confidence level autonomous action should pause pending human input. Comms-Degraded Behavior and Store-and-Forward Link loss should trigger pre-planned behavior, not paralysis. Architectures that rely on continuous connectivity will fail in any contested environment. Comms-degraded design patterns include: pre-mission intent loading (platforms know the mission plan and can execute autonomously within it during blackout), store-and-forward relay (platforms carry messages across intermittent links and deliver when connectivity briefly restores), and behavioral contracts (agents commit to predictable responses to specific events, allowing peers to anticipate their actions without real-time coordination). The design question is how long a formation can operate coherently on pre-loaded intent before divergence in world state requires resynchronization.

chunks.title: Autonomous Swarm Coordination | Architecture Concepts | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Inter-Platform Deconfliction
chunks.text: Inter-Platform Deconfliction As platforms maneuver independently in shared airspace or terrain, deconfliction becomes safety-critical. Static separation rules are insufficient when platforms respond dynamically to environment changes. Reactive collision avoidance algorithms (velocity obstacles, reciprocal velocity obstacles (RVO), and potential-field methods) allow real-time path adjustment without centralized coordination. For air systems operating in three-dimensional space, temporal deconfliction (staggered timing through shared waypoints) complements spatial separation. Task deconfliction (ensuring two platforms do not redundantly engage the same target or clear the same area) requires distributed task allocation mechanisms such as consensus-based bundle algorithms (CBBA) that converge on consistent assignment across the formation. Human Supervisory Control and Authority Boundaries Autonomous swarms operating within federal programs require explicit authority boundaries: what the formation may decide autonomously, what requires human confirmation, and what must halt pending operator instruction. These boundaries are not just policy; they shape architecture. Supervisory interfaces must convey formation state, individual platform health, and pending decisions at a scan rate an operator can actually manage across a multi-platform formation. Adjustable autonomy patterns (where the operator can fluidly shift authority levels between platforms or sub-formations) allow mission flexibility while preserving accountability. Designing for human-on-the-loop oversight is a first-class architectural constraint, not a post-hoc addition.

chunks.title: Neural Network Optimization for Tactical Edge AI | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Neural Network Optimization for Tactical Edge AI
chunks.text: Neural Network Optimization for Tactical Edge AI Insights Technical Publications Neural Network Optimization A Ravonics architectural perspective on running capable AI where bandwidth, power, and connectivity are scarce Federal missions increasingly demand capable AI inference at the tactical edge: on the platform, the sensor, or the dismounted device, not in a distant data center. Operators work in denied, degraded, intermittent, and limited (DDIL) conditions where the network cannot be assumed, latency budgets are unforgiving, and the decision must be made locally or not at all. The cloud-first assumptions that govern commercial machine learning simply do not hold once connectivity becomes a contested resource. This creates a central engineering tension. The most capable models are large, power-hungry, and memory-intensive, while edge hardware offers a fixed and modest budget of compute, memory bandwidth, and watts. Closing that gap is not a matter of buying a bigger accelerator; it is a discipline of model optimization. The sections below preview the techniques Ravonics weighs when architecting inference for constrained, mission-critical environments. Quantization Quantization represents weights and activations at lower numerical precision, moving from 32-bit floating point toward 8-bit integers or below. The payoff is smaller models, lower memory bandwidth, and faster arithmetic on edge accelerators built for integer math. Post-training quantization is fast to apply; quantization-aware training preserves more accuracy by simulating reduced precision during fine-tuning. The architectural decision is where precision can be safely lowered without crossing a mission-relevant accuracy floor.

chunks.title: Neural Network Optimization for Tactical Edge AI | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Structured & Unstructured Pruning
chunks.text: Structured & Unstructured Pruning Pruning removes parameters that contribute little to a model's output. Unstructured pruning zeroes individual weights for high theoretical sparsity, but realizing speedups requires hardware and kernels that exploit sparse computation. Structured pruning removes whole channels, filters, or attention heads, yielding dense smaller models that run faster on commodity edge silicon without special support. The trade is granularity versus deployability: a choice driven by the target accelerator, not by the metric alone. Knowledge Distillation Distillation trains a compact student model to reproduce the behavior of a larger, more capable teacher, learning from the teacher's soft probability outputs and intermediate representations rather than labels alone. A well-distilled student can retain much of the teacher's capability at a fraction of the parameter count and inference cost. For tactical edge use, distillation lets a heavyweight model developed in the rear inform a lean, deployable model that fits the platform's actual power and memory envelope. Mixture-of-Experts & Conditional Compute Mixture-of-experts architectures hold large total capacity but activate only a small subset of expert sub-networks per input, so compute scales with what a given inference actually needs rather than with the full parameter count. Combined with conditional and early-exit strategies that stop computation once confidence is sufficient, this delivers capacity without paying full activation cost on every token or frame: a meaningful advantage when energy and thermal headroom at the edge are strictly bounded.

chunks.title: Neural Network Optimization for Tactical Edge AI | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Hardware-Aware Compilation & Accelerator Targeting
chunks.text: Hardware-Aware Compilation & Accelerator Targeting An optimized model still underperforms if the deployment stack ignores the silicon beneath it. Hardware-aware compilation maps operations onto the target accelerator (GPU, NPU, DSP, or FPGA) through graph fusion, memory-layout tuning, operator selection, and kernel specialization. The same network can vary several-fold in latency and energy depending on how it is compiled and scheduled. Treating the compiler and runtime as first-class architectural concerns is what turns a theoretically small model into a genuinely fast one on real edge hardware. Accuracy / Latency Governance Every optimization trades some fidelity for speed and footprint, so the degradation must be measured, not assumed. Governance means benchmarking compressed models against full-precision baselines on mission-representative data, setting explicit accuracy and latency thresholds the deployment must meet, and instrumenting drift detection in the field. Where stakes are high, human review gates keep an operator in the loop before consequential action. Optimization is only complete when its costs are quantified and bounded to mission-acceptable limits. Want to discuss edge AI architecture for your program? chunks.title: Zero Trust Implementation for Federal Networks | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Zero Trust Implementation for Federal Networks
chunks.text: Zero Trust Implementation for Federal Networks Insights Technical Publications Zero Trust for Federal Networks A Ravonics perspective on treating trust as a posture to be continuously earned, not a perimeter to be defended Zero trust is a direct response to the collapse of the network perimeter. In a federal landscape of cloud workloads, remote operators, and mobile endpoints, the old assumption that everything inside the firewall is safe no longer holds. The operating principle becomes "never trust, always verify": every request for access is authenticated, authorized, and evaluated against context, regardless of where it originates or what it has reached before. The federal community has codified this shift in NIST SP 800-207, and successive executive direction has made zero trust an expectation rather than an aspiration. Aligning to that guidance gives agencies a shared vocabulary and a defensible reference architecture. A mandate alone, however, stalls without architectural foundations. Zero trust is not a product to be purchased or a single appliance to be installed; it is a set of design decisions that must be wired through identity, network, workload, and data layers together. The sections below outline the pillars Ravonics treats as load-bearing when helping federal teams move from intent to an enforceable posture.

chunks.title: Zero Trust Implementation for Federal Networks | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Identity as the New Perimeter
chunks.text: Identity as the New Perimeter When the network boundary dissolves, identity becomes the control plane. A mature ICAM foundation (strong, phishing-resistant authentication, granular authorization, and rigorous lifecycle governance for both human and non-human accounts) is the precondition for every other zero-trust decision. Each access request is evaluated against the verified identity behind it, never against its network location. Micro-Segmentation & Least-Privilege Access Flat networks let a single foothold become free movement. Micro-segmentation divides the environment into small, independently governed zones so that compromise of one workload does not imply access to the next. Paired with least-privilege policy (access scoped to the specific resource, for the specific task, for the minimum duration), it shrinks the blast radius of any breach to its smallest practical size. Continuous Verification & Device Posture Trust granted once is not trust granted forever. Continuous verification re-evaluates each session against live signals: the health and patch state of the device, the sensitivity of the resource, and behavioral context that may indicate compromise. Device posture becomes a first-class input, so an endpoint that drifts out of compliance can have its access reduced or revoked without manual intervention. Policy-as-Code & Automated Enforcement Access policy expressed in prose drifts from access policy as enforced. Encoding authorization rules as version-controlled, testable code makes intent explicit, reviewable, and auditable. Automated enforcement then applies those policies uniformly across services, closing the gap between what a control document says and what the running system actually permits, and giving assessors a traceable record of every change.

chunks.title: Zero Trust Implementation for Federal Networks | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Immutable Infrastructure & GitOps
chunks.text: Immutable Infrastructure & GitOps Servers patched in place accumulate undocumented state that erodes trust. Immutable infrastructure replaces rather than mutates components, so every workload is rebuilt from a known, signed definition. Managed through GitOps, the desired state lives in version control and is reconciled automatically, making configuration drift visible, rollback deterministic, and the environment itself a verifiable enabler of zero trust. Telemetry, Analytics & Continuous Monitoring Zero trust depends on seeing what is actually happening. Comprehensive telemetry across identity, network, and workload feeds analytics that distinguish normal operation from emerging threat. Sustained over time, this continuous monitoring supports a continuous-ATO posture: where authorization is maintained through ongoing evidence rather than a point-in-time snapshot that ages the moment it is signed. chunks.heading: Zero Trust Architecture: Why Mandates Stall Without Architectural Foundation
chunks.text: Zero Trust Architecture: Why Mandates Stall Without Architectural Foundation Insights Industry Perspectives Zero Trust Mandates A Ravonics cybersecurity policy perspective on why zero trust executive mandates stall when identity and ICAM foundation isn't in place first, and the architectural patterns that make adoption practical The federal zero trust mandate is unambiguous. OMB Memorandum M-22-09 set specific capability targets for federal civilian agencies. CISA's Zero Trust Maturity Model provides the five-pillar framework against which agencies are expected to measure progress. DoW has its own Zero Trust Strategy with 91 target activities. The policy signal has never been clearer, the deadlines have never been firmer, and the political will (forged in the aftermath of SolarWinds and the Log4Shell disclosure wave) has never been stronger. Yet agency programs implementing zero trust repeatedly stall, overspend, and underdeliver against their own roadmaps. The reason is almost always the same: the underlying identity and access management foundation was never built. Zero trust is not a product. It is an architectural posture that requires a specific set of operational capabilities to exist before the posture can be meaningfully enforced. Buying a software-defined perimeter solution or a microsegmentation platform without those foundational capabilities in place does not move an agency toward zero trust; it adds expensive complexity to a perimeter-dependent environment while providing a veneer of compliance on paper. The following six dimensions trace the architectural preconditions and sequencing decisions that determine whether a zero trust adoption program achieves real posture change or generates impressive slide decks and stalled pilots.

chunks.title: Zero Trust Architecture: Why Mandates Stall Without Architectural Foundation | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Identity Is the New Perimeter, and It Must Come First
chunks.text: Identity Is the New Perimeter, and It Must Come First NIST SP 800-207's core zero trust principle is that no request is implicitly trusted based on network location. Trust is instead established through continuous verification of identity, device health, and context at the time of each access request. This means the identity infrastructure (authoritative identity stores, credential lifecycle management, multi-factor authentication, and the policy decision point that evaluates each access request) must be fully operational before any other zero trust pillar can function correctly. Agencies that skip identity maturation and jump to network segmentation or data tagging build a governance system with no reliable subject to govern. Identity is not one pillar among five; it is the load-bearing foundation beneath all of them. ICAM Modernization Is the Hardest Part of the Journey Identity, Credential, and Access Management modernization is consistently the longest-lead element of any federal zero trust program. It requires rationalizing identity stores accumulated across decades of mergers, reorganizations, and siloed system deployments; retiring or federating legacy directories; implementing PIV/CAC enforcement for privileged access; and deploying a policy enforcement infrastructure that can evaluate rich context attributes (device compliance posture, time, location, behavior anomalies), not just username and password. Most agencies underestimate ICAM scope by a factor of two to three when they write their zero trust roadmaps. Programs that sequence ICAM first, accept the longer timeline, and resist pressure to show early "zero trust wins" through network products consistently outperform those that chase visible deliverables while ICAM remains immature.

chunks.title: Zero Trust Architecture: Why Mandates Stall Without Architectural Foundation | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Device Health Verification Requires a Managed Endpoint Baseline
chunks.text: Device Health Verification Requires a Managed Endpoint Baseline Zero trust access policy evaluates device health as a trust signal alongside user identity. A device that fails patch compliance, lacks EDR coverage, or cannot attest its configuration state should receive degraded or denied access regardless of the user's credentials. Enforcing this requires a complete and current inventory of every managed endpoint, continuous compliance assessment, and the ability to pass device health signals to the policy decision point in real time. Agencies with fragmented endpoint management (common where IT has been federated across bureaus or components) frequently discover that they cannot enumerate their own device population before they can begin enforcing device-based access policy. Endpoint inventory and MDM consolidation are unglamorous prerequisites that block zero trust progress when they are absent. Network Microsegmentation Follows Data Classification Microsegmentation (dividing the network into fine-grained zones with explicit allow policies between them) is one of the most visible zero trust capabilities and one of the most frequently sequenced in the wrong order. Effective microsegmentation requires knowing what data lives where, what its sensitivity classification is, and which workloads legitimately need to communicate with which other workloads. Without data discovery and classification upstream, microsegmentation boundaries are drawn around topology rather than around data sensitivity, producing segments that are technically enforced but strategically arbitrary. The network pillar of zero trust is downstream of the data pillar, even though network products are easier to procure and demonstrate in a briefing.

chunks.title: Zero Trust Architecture: Why Mandates Stall Without Architectural Foundation | Ravonics
chunks.heading: Continuous Monitoring Closes the Loop Between Policy and Reality
chunks.text: Continuous Monitoring Closes the Loop Between Policy and Reality Zero trust is not a state achieved at a point in time; it is a continuous process of evaluating context, enforcing policy, detecting anomalies, and adjusting trust levels dynamically. This requires a security operations capability that ingests telemetry from identity systems, endpoints, network flows, and application logs and correlates them against access policy in near real time. Agencies that implement zero trust controls without investing in the monitoring infrastructure to detect policy violations and anomalous access patterns have built a fence with no camera. The mandate language around continuous monitoring is frequently underweighted in program plans relative to its operational importance; it is the mechanism that makes zero trust a living posture rather than a compliance checkbox. Compliance Theater Versus Genuine Posture Change The most insidious failure mode in federal zero trust adoption is meeting CISA ZTMM milestone language while the underlying architecture remains implicitly trust-based. An agency can deploy a proxy that nominally enforces MFA on application access while leaving lateral movement paths wide open across a flat internal network. It can mark a capability as "advanced" on a maturity self-assessment while the policy decision point enforces static rules rather than dynamic, context-sensitive evaluation. Program offices and oversight bodies should evaluate zero trust progress against observed access behavior and red-team results, not against capability deployment checklists alone. Genuine posture change is measurable: it reduces the blast radius of a compromised credential, limits lateral movement, and accelerates detection of anomalous access. Compliance theater does none of these things.

chunks.title: Privacy Policy | Ravonics LLC
chunks.heading: Privacy Policy
chunks.text: Privacy Policy Home Privacy Policy Legal Privacy Policy Effective Date: August 22, 2026 Ravonics LLC ("Ravonics," "we," "us," or "our") operates the website at ravonics.com (the "Site"). This Privacy Policy explains what information we collect through the Site, how we use it, and your choices regarding that information. By using the Site or submitting information through our forms, you agree to the practices described here. 1. Information We Collect The Site is an informational marketing website. We do not collect personal information through passive browsing: no tracking cookies or third-party advertising scripts are deployed on this Site (see Section 4). We collect information only when you voluntarily submit one of our three website forms: Contact Form (contact.html) The general contact form collects: Contact name Business email address Phone number Free-text message RFP / RFI Intake Form (booking.html) The RFP / RFI intake form collects the following in addition to the contact details above: Organization / Agency name and type Title / role of the submitting point of contact Areas of interest (capability or solution type; checkbox selection) Solicitation or RFP / RFI number (if applicable) Contract vehicle and set-aside type NAICS code for the requirement Estimated contract value (budget range) Period of performance and proposal due date Supporting documents attached to the submission (unclassified only) Free-text project and scope summary (unclassified)

chunks.title: Privacy Policy | Ravonics LLC
chunks.heading: Capability Update Form (company/doing-business.html)
chunks.text: Capability Update Form (company/doing-business.html) The capability update form collects: Name Work email address Agency or organization (optional) Primary area of interest (optional) All fields collected through these forms relate exclusively to professional and business inquiries. We do not request sensitive personal information (e.g., Social Security numbers, financial account details, health information). 2. How We Process Your Information Information you submit is transmitted securely and stored in our customer-relationship systems, accessible only to authorized Ravonics personnel for the purpose of responding to your inquiry. We use this information solely to: Respond to your inquiry or request Evaluate whether and how Ravonics may be able to assist with your requirement Maintain a record of business-development contacts consistent with federal-contractor relationship management practices We do not use your information for automated decision-making or profiling. If you use the capability update form, we may use the contact details you provide to send the requested business and capability updates; you may ask us to stop at any time. 3. Federal Procurement Inquiries Ravonics is a SAM.gov-registered federal contractor (UEI: YCBDVKN1A9G7). Information submitted through the booking form in connection with a federal procurement inquiry is handled with heightened care. We treat such submissions as business-sensitive communications, share them only with personnel who have a need to know for the purpose of responding to your inquiry, and do not use them for any purpose unrelated to that inquiry. If your inquiry involves controlled unclassified information (CUI) or other sensitive government information, please do not transmit that information through our website forms. Contact us directly at contact@ravonics.com to arrange a suitable channel.

chunks.title: Privacy Policy | Ravonics LLC
chunks.heading: 4. Cookies, Analytics, and Tracking
chunks.text: 4. Cookies, Analytics, and Tracking This Site does not use third-party advertising or tracking cookies. No data is shared with third-party analytics or advertising platforms. 5. Data Sharing We do not sell, rent, or trade your personal information. We share it only in the following limited circumstances: Service providers: We engage third-party service providers who assist us in operating our systems and processing your submissions. These providers are bound by appropriate data protection obligations and are not permitted to use your information for their own purposes. Legal obligation: We may disclose information if required to do so by applicable law, regulation, court order, or lawful government request. Business transfers: If Ravonics is acquired, merges, or transfers substantially all of its assets, submitted information may be transferred as part of that transaction, subject to the same privacy protections described here. 6. Data Retention We retain information submitted through our forms for as long as necessary to fulfill the purpose for which it was collected: including responding to your inquiry, managing a potential or ongoing business relationship, and meeting applicable legal and contractual record-keeping obligations. When information is no longer needed for those purposes, we delete or de-identify it in accordance with our internal data governance practices.

chunks.title: Privacy Policy | Ravonics LLC
chunks.heading: 7. Security
chunks.text: 7. Security We apply reasonable administrative and technical safeguards to protect the information you submit. Form submissions are transmitted over TLS-encrypted HTTPS connections and stored in secured systems subject to enterprise-grade access controls. No method of electronic transmission or storage is perfectly secure, however, and we cannot guarantee absolute security. If you believe your information has been compromised, please contact us at contact@ravonics.com . 8. Your Choices You may contact us at any time to: Request access to the personal information we hold about you Request correction of inaccurate information Request deletion of your information, subject to any legal or contractual retention requirements To exercise any of these rights, email us at contact@ravonics.com with the subject line "Privacy Request." We will respond within a reasonable time. 9. Children This Site is not directed to children under the age of 13, and we do not knowingly collect personal information from children. If you believe a child has submitted information through this Site, please contact us and we will promptly delete it. 10. Changes to This Policy We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time. When we do, we will revise the Effective Date at the top of this page. We encourage you to review this Policy periodically. Continued use of the Site after changes are posted constitutes acceptance of the revised Policy. 11. Contact Us For questions or concerns about this Privacy Policy or our data practices, contact: Mailing Address Ravonics LLC, 313 Walnut St, Ravenswood, WV 26164 Email contact@ravonics.com Phone +1 (304) 927-2600 View our Terms of Use → Ready to Deploy Next-Gen Technology? Submit RFP / RFI

HUBZone sole source FAR 19.1306 For nonmanufacturing requirements, the ceiling is $5.5 million including options. chunks.heading: Method and source fields.
chunks.text: Method and source fields. This is a static reading of one captured edition. The source file is the durable handoff for the exact rows, values, and page numbers behind this page. Included in the calculation Rows from pages[] , grouped by their recorded section . Main-zone totals only where layout.hasMainContent is true. Words from seo.wordCountMain , images from media.imgContent , and summed HTML section counts. One-decimal display rounding for averages; source integers remain the basis of every total. Excluded from this measurement No traffic, search demand, conversions, social sentiment, or visitor analytics. No judgment of visual quality, readability, contrast, focus order, keyboard traps, or screen-reader experience. No claim that the captured rows represent every page currently reachable on the live site. No inference that an amber rollup is a defect without reading its page-level reason. Read related work Engage with team Eight editions · 36 designed pages each Reports built for a decision, not a download counter Each edition has a reader decision, methodology, counterpoints, visual cadence, accessible HTML, and a downloadable print artifact. The HTML edition remains canonical. B01 · 36 pages AI Risk in Mission Decision Systems AI risk becomes governable when lifecycle evidence, decision authority, uncertainty, and recourse are designed together. Read HTML edition · Download PDF B02 · 36 pages Zero Trust and CUI Boundaries Zero trust and CUI protection meet at explicit resource, identity, data, and assessment boundaries. Read HTML edition · Download PDF B03 · 36 pages Post-Quantum Migration Field Guide Post-quantum migration is an inventory, dependency, validation, and replacement program before it is an algorithm-selection exercise. Read HTML edition · Download PDF B04 · 36 pages Tactical Edge AI Evaluation Edge AI evaluation must join model behavior to power, timing, connectivity, thermal, security, and sustainment evidence. Read HTML edition · Download PDF B05 · 36 pages JADC2 Interoperability by Design Interoperability is a maintained relationship across semantics, timing, authority, trust, and failure behavior. Read HTML edition · Download PDF B06 · 36 pages

chunks.title: Vulnerability disclosure policy
chunks.heading: Vulnerability disclosure policy
chunks.text: Report a suspected vulnerability in a Ravonics public website safely. Vulnerability disclosure policy How to report a security vulnerability in ravonics.com to Ravonics LLC, what is in scope, and what we ask of researchers. Read related work Engage with team Vulnerability disclosure · ravonics.com Report a vulnerability If you believe you have found a security vulnerability in a Ravonics public website, email contact@ravonics.com with "Security" in the subject line. Our machine-readable contact record is published at /.well-known/security.txt (RFC 9116). Helpful reports include: The affected URL and a description of the issue and its likely impact. Steps to reproduce it, with any request, payload or screenshot needed to follow them. How we can reach you for follow-up questions, and whether you would like public credit. Scope In scope: ravonics.com and its pages, files and public forms. Out of scope: third-party services the site links to or embeds, denial-of-service testing, social engineering, physical testing, and findings from automated scanners without a demonstrated impact. chunks.title: Trust center
chunks.heading: Trust center
chunks.text: Check who Ravonics is, how the site handles your data, and how to report a problem. Trust center Ravonics LLC registrations, security posture, data handling for website forms, accessibility conformance and vulnerability disclosure in one place. Read related work Engage with team Trust center · Ravonics LLC Who we are Ravonics LLC, 313 Walnut St, Ravenswood, WV 26164. Founded 2026. SAM.gov registered (Active). UEI YCBDVKN1A9G7. CAGE Code 20DS8. SBA HUBZone Certified, verifiable through SAM.gov and the SBA Dynamic Small Business Search. NAICS 541512, 541330, 541715. Security posture Certifications held: SBA HUBZone only. NIST SP 800-171 alignment is underway and a CMMC assessment is planned; Ravonics holds no CMMC certification and no FedRAMP authorization. Our founder holds an active U.S. Public Trust. We do not perform classified work. This website is a static site served over HTTPS. Its pages carry a Content-Security-Policy, and every change passes automated quality, accessibility and dependency-audit checks before it is published. Do not send classified, controlled unclassified (CUI) or export-controlled information through this website or its forms. Data handling for website forms Browsing the site sets no tracking or advertising cookies. We receive information only when you submit the contact form, the RFP / RFI intake form or the capability update form: What we collect: your name, organization, role, email and phone, your message, and for the RFP / RFI form the solicitation details and any documents you attach. How it travels: over HTTPS to a Ravonics-operated intake service in Microsoft Azure, which checks the submission with Cloudflare Turnstile and rate limits, then records it as a business inquiry in our customer relationship management system. Who sees it: only the Ravonics staff responding to your inquiry. We do not sell or share it for marketing. The privacy policy has the full terms, including retention and your choices.
